MESSRS. WATTS AND CO.'S HUGH XMAS BAZAAR Will flash its joyous light into the Nurseries of every home on the banks of the Mersey. This Grande Fayre will bee holden in Compton House, Liverpool, on MONDAY NEXT. the 14th inst., and the followynge clayey, with moste delightfulle merriement, when alle folkes may come and buy ye mania euriouse Rickshaws. Baubles, Knicknackeries, and divers other thynges shall be then displayed on ye different counters, and bee treated by ye faire Ladyes and others in charge thereof with much gracious- nesse and honorifica.bilitudinitie. GOD SAVE THE QUEEN. As Xmas Festivities are approached and Cooks wait anxiously to fill the domestic larder in preparation for the on- coming tournament of teeth, Messrs. Watts and Co. provide amusements for the nursery. GOD BLESS THE PRINCE OF WALES In this Great Fair the Comic Element will be sustained by the clamorous chatter and squeak of Mechancial Toys, and those denizens of the animal kingdom whose organs of speech are imperfectly developed. Thee will be GRAND EQUESTRIAN MANCEUVRES By Rocking Horses, GLITTERING SCENES OF PAGEANTRY On the Way to the Grotto, ALL-DAY RECEPTIONS BY FATHER XMAS. Brilliant Spectacles in the Doll Saloon. Engagement of a Troupe of Celestial Fairies. A Splendid Stud of Beautiful Horses and Ponies will be sold to the first comers. All thoroughly broken and unequalled for condition and excellence of training. The Stud Includes Stool Horses from 3s. 6d., Safety Swing Horses, and a choice of Cobs, Hacks. Hunters, and Racers, sharpened for frost and warranted not to stumble. Buffalo Bill Model on Horse, 7s. 6d. Large Models, 6s. lid., 9s. 11d., 12s. 9d., 18s. ed. RULE BRITANNIA.. 0 YEZ 1 0 YRZ ! OUM ! FATHER CHRISTMAS AND THR GROTTO I THE DEAR OLD GROTTO. Loved Abode of Father Christmas and the Fairies—the Most Charming Spot in the Universe. ADMISSION SIXPENCE. For which the Fairies will give a surprising Pack, t of Toys worth a Jew's Ransom In the eyes of the recipients. And now, having visited the Grotto, the Young Adventurer will be ready for AN ALLIGATOR STORY. The "Daily Teltgraph " recently informed the world that enormous numbers of Alligators were frisking in the swamps and lakes bordering the great River Amazon. The " Daily Telegraph" was imperfectly informed, for net only Alligators, but Beasts, Birds, Fishes, and Reptiles of all sorts were assem- bled there, awaiting transport to COMPTON HOUSE WORLD'S FAIR. And are now securely housed in Noah's Arks, Circuses" Menageries, Butchers' Shops, or led by Organ Grinders in the Fair for the entertainment of Messrs. Watts and Co.'s young friends. "A Living Dog is better than a Dead Lion," says an old proverb—don't believe it, the Stuffed Lions in Comp- ton House Noah's Arks are better than any Living Dog. These Noah's Arks of all sizes and shapes are numerous enough to rescue all the families of Lancashire, Cheshire, and North Wales from any Flood of Ennui that may threaten them dur - ing the Xmas Festival. itLEPHANTS, COWS, DOGS, SHEEP, DONKEYS, And other well-known Quadrupeds will be found in the Fai and may be expected by good behaviour and general attrar' tiveness to win the hearts and open the purses of the Little- Ladies and Gentlemen of Liverpool. The Fur Dogs offer themselves at 60 and Hid. The Woolly Sheep only stipulate that they must not be cut tip into mutton chops for breakfast. The Dogs also guaran- tee that their owners may sleep securely at night undisturbed by burglarious marauders. "I remember," says Varley, the water-colour painter, " the last time I was tossed by a Mad Bull—." Mr. Varley's experiences were not at Compton bus a, for the Millennium reigns there and all creation is as happy as in Eden. CHRISTMAS TREE ORNAMENTS Are full of the SP/EIT 01 SANTA CLAUS, and obtrude them- selves everywhere, determined that their ancient patron shall find his way into every family. Who can count the stars of heaven ? Neither can memory recount all the wonders and. attractions of this fair. There are MECHANICAL TOYS, SCIENTIFIC TOYS, Musical Toys, Comical Toys, Soft Toys, for Babies, Toy, Books, Toy Swings, Toys for Young Sportsmen, and Soldiers' Barracks, complete withcastle and soldiers, 21s 6d; smaller, , les 9d. Building Bricks of all sorts and sizes. Pistols and Targets. is Rifles, very strong, 6s 64. Horses and Carts from is ild,• Mechanical Engines, 50, 1044, is 11d. Fire Engine, with mechanical whistle, 2s 6d. Figures, comical and otherwise, Soldiers, Sailors, Clowns, Columbines, and types of all sorts and conditions of men. , Tool Boxes, Picture Blocks, Kaleidoscopes. Banks, Rail- ways (Express Trains and Stopping Trains), Magic Lanterns, Musical Boxes, Tambourines, Banjos, Kettledrums, and all other sorts of musical instruments, big and little, capable of producing noise enough to make the planets, "for over singing as they shine," step to listen. THE WORLD'S DOLL PAIR. CHICAGO ANTICIPATED BY COMPTON HOUSE, LIVERPOOL. WAX DOLLS, RAG DOLLS, BLACK AND WHITE DOLLS. All Fair and Mild as a Vernal Sun. Messrs. WATTS and CO.'S Challenge for an International Exhibition of the most beautiful Dolls in creation was ac- cepted by the sovereign people everywhere. Hindostan. Japan, China, Fairyland, and Africa have sent contingents of their choicest beauties, and 'twill be for visitors to say 'whether those or the rosy-cheeked English Dolls are the most charming. There are WOODEN DOLLS, DOLLS WITH REAL HAIR. LITTLE RED RIDING HOOD DOLLS. MODEL DOLLS FROM MUNICH, AT is. OM, These Dolls are sure to be loved wherever they go; and the radiancethe love of a doll throws around a nursery exceeds all other except —the Electric Light at Compton House. THE REAL FRENCH DOLLS. Arajointecl, with and without closing eves, have real Hair. and Mohair, are both dressed and undressed, and can talk •

DOLLS DRESSED IN SILK AND SATIN Are most lovable Dolls, but don't love them to distraction as Romeo loved Juliet, and when he lost her ordered poithorses and poison, but love wisely, and well enough to buy one. EM4IA, GWENDOLINE, AND FANNY Are talking Dolls; at surprising beauty. If, like Wordsworth' you come within the sound of Emma's voice, don't like him, be over-cautious of the attendant risk, but—buy at once and take it home.

SAILOR DOLLS Are popular in Liverpcol, they don't talk much, yet are full of sprightly wit, and constantly remind us that" Britannia rules the waves." Once again let the feast on the table appear, Let the music and dancing come after; Oh, joyfully, peacefully, endeth the year, For Christmas is here with his laughter. Let him come in, Let him come in, Give him a welcome in every home ; Give hirn,ta welcome where'er he maycome ; i Open your doors and let him come n. He is here with his promise and pleasure again, With his scenes and his memories tender; And, oh, may the musings which come in his train Some kindness and goodness engender. Let him come in, Let him come in, - Send him not forth all unowned and ignored' • Find him a place by the hearth and the board; Open your hearts and let him come in. SAM WOOD.

(From "Fun Almanac.") MORE GOOD ADVICE GONE WRONG. DOROTHEA (the disappointed).—" I hear, Julia darling, that Lord Broadlands has proposed to you. My dear, he has by no means a good reputation. If I were you I should hesitate before accepting him." JULIA (the jubilant).—" Dearest, if you were I, there would be no need for hesitation, because—he wouldn't propose."

Weather prognostication for 1892.—1 t can't be worse than it was in 1891. DREADFUL OUTRAGE.—Featherhead made an appoint- ment last Thursday to meet a friend at the top of S. Paul's and then threw him over. Why are comic journalists public benefactors in the matter of the Income Tax? Because they are always "taking it off." ARTISTIC.—When a lawyer draws a deed, can it be described as a limn of the law? Why should a woman be wary of marrying a bald headed man? Because, no matter how, badly he may turn out, there is no parting with him.
NO-EL-IMINATION NEEDED. We call it Christmas, but the Gaul The word doth differently spell ; That season he doth Noel call— Our spelling doth include No" 1." THE MISTLETOE BOUGH.

Jones thought he was keeping up old Christmas cus- toms when he hung up the mistletoe in his hall. But it happened that Mrs. Jones was going downstairs that morning en deshabille' to get something in the kitchen !or the baby. The sweep was in that morning, and was coming up the stairs. In the dim, religious light, he kitsed Mrs. Jones under the mistletoe, because he thought she was the new parlourmaid. There was a shine in the tents of Shem that would have lit up the _Thames Embankment and the shot towers apposite.

TO SWEEP A HALFPENNY OUT OF THE HAND. This seems a very easy trick, but if done fairly it is 2 really difficult. Open the hand naturally and place the halfpenny on the palm; then ask some one to brash it out with a whisk-broom. After repeated efforts, it will probably be suspected 'that the halfpenny is fastened in your hand in some -way. In order to prove that it is not, let the sweeper place it on his own palm, and he will find it remains as immovable there as when he tried to sweep it from the hand of the other peisons. A few persons have flat palms. The halfpenny may easily be swept off such palms, but they are not common

TO PICK UP AN APPLE WITH A SPOON. It requires not a little patience to accomplish this ' trick. Place a large, round apple, stem up, on a smooth floor; then try to take it up with a spoon. The very • effort of trying to get the epoon under the apple starts it rolling; to the amusement of the onlookers. If done quickly enough, the apple can be taken up while in • motion ; but the proper way is to wait until it ceases to roll, and then carefully push the spoon far enough under • the apple to get the centre of gravity over the spoon, when there is no difficulty in picking it up. TO CUT AN ATTLE WITHOUT BREAKING THE SKIN. Thread a needle with strong thread. Insert the needle • just under the skin of the apple, take a stitch, and care- fully draw the needle and thread through to within six or seven inches of the end. Then insert the needle aglin, this time in the exact hole it was withdrawn from. Continue the stitches in this manner around the apDle, --withdrawing the needle the last time through the first hole made. The thread is entirely around the apple now, concealed by its skin. Take a firm hold of each • end of the thread and, holding both of the ends well to- gether, to prevent tearing the skin, pull gently. The thread cuts it way slowly through the apple until it is in two pieces, when tlie thread is withdrawn through the tiny hole made by the needle. If this trick is done carefully enough, the breaks in the skin will not be discernible on the closest inspection. _lndeed, the only convincing proof that the apple has been cut in half, will be to pare a narrow strip of skin -where the needle and thread have travelled, when the =apple will fall apart.—Prom "Old and Young." * * *

div.head: LONELY CHRISTMAS EVE, AND HOW IT ENDED.
div.p: A LONELY CHRISTMAS EVE, AND HOW IT ENDED.

It is Christmas Eve. lam sitting alone in my Temple Chambers, feeling deadly dull; every now and then comes the muffled sound of wheels over the snow that lies thick in Middle Temple Lane. I suppose lam the only poor devil in this house in chambers to-night—all the rest have gone home to their own homes, or the homes of relatives and friends, where lightness, light, and laughter are reigning supreme. I have no home— only chambers. Yet—no; there is another lonely man in this house. From the chambers above comes the sound, the sweet, soft sound of a flute exquisitely played. As the silver and mellow notes float upon the silent night I feel sadder than ever, my eyes begin to moisten, and. confound it! there is a big lump in my throat. I relight my pipe mid listen still, 4 I begin to think of last Christmas, and the jolly time f 4iad at Hallfellow Hall. She was there—she, of the 'wavy brown hair, the laughing eyes, the dark little dimples round her mouth; 'the sweetest, dearest, dain- tiest, queenliest, little flirt that ever made a man's heart leap and fall and ache. Before Twelfth night we had quarrelled and parted. She had given too many smiles to Benjamin Bullion, that embodiment of wealthy pompous snobbery. I had only a heart to offer her, but, confound it if my heart Was not worth her having she need not have broken it. Still that flute ripples and ripples adown the silent gloomy old stairway and the dark corridor, and I feel gadder and sadder. I wonder by-and-by, if the other fellow is sad and lonely too. I don't know him. I have 'only just moVed in here and haven't even got my name Qg o 1 Y" natio I LllAdie eases. His oak is banged; he comes blundering downstairs with a portmanteau, for I can bear it hump on the stairs. Lucky dog; he's off Lome- where, to play his flute to a livelier audience. I wonder I what sort of a feilow he is. just step out and have a look at him notwithstanding etiquette, and all that sort of rot. So I stride to the door, and shout to the man going downstairs: - "Thanks for your Music, sir. Can I help you down- stairs with your traps ?" "Hallo he laughs. angel unawares ?" " Entertaining a miserable wretch," I mutter, sotto voce. He has reached the bottom stair. He turns. The light falls on his face. It is her brother. "Harry !" "Dick!" We are shaking hands and laughing at the idea of has- 1 ling, been neighbours for a week without knowing it, for hile.is only borrowing the chambers upstairs, and his name too, is absent from the door posts. "Good-bye, Harry, old man; you'll miss your train." "-blot I," he replies. 'Look here, old man, come down to Hailfellow Hall with me." I shake my bead. "Come along, old boy," he persists. "We've such a jolly party. She'll be so glad to see you." I waver. • She will, really," he goes on. " She's been moping like an owl since your tiff. It was through you she re- fused Bullion. She told the mater she could never care for anybody but you." Igo ; I scramble my traps together. Talk about a Merry Christmas--- I ! --From "Ally Sloper's Christmas Holidays."

UR GLADSTONE'S JOURNEY TO BIARRITZ. Mr. and,Mrs. Oladstone, accompanied by Mr. John Morley, Miss Gladstone,and Mr.Armithead, left Charing- cross Station, London,on Tuesday morning at ten o'clock, en route for Paris and Biarritz. The right hon. gentle- man arrived at the station with Mrs. Gladstone in a closed carriage at a quarter to ten. He was recognised immediately by the fairly numerous body of persons who had gathered behind the barriers, and who cheered him enthusiastically. Mr. Gladstone,who wore a large travel- ling cloak trimmed with sealskin fur, seemed in the best of 'health and spirits. He frequently acknowledged the salutations of the people, and joined in animated conver- sation with the members of the party and several friends who came to see him off. Amongst the latter were Mr. and Mrs. Henry Gladstone Lord Oxenbridge, Sir El. Watkin, M.P. Mr. E. w. Hamilton (a former private secretary), and Sir Algernon West. Punctually at ten o'clock the signal for the train to start was given, and amidst general cheering and waving of handkerchiefs it left the station. Mr. Gladstone acknowledged the cheer- ing by repeatedly bowing from the carriage window. The right hon. gentleman and his friends left Folke- stone by the midday boat. Be was cheered by the crowd on the quay. Boutoorm, TIIESDAT.—Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, accom- panied by Miss Gladstone and Mr. John Morley, arrived here by the Louise Dagmar from Folkestone at 1 50 p.m. to-day, and as they landed cheers were raised by the people on the quay. The distinguished party imme- diately entered a special saloon train which was waiting, and left at 2 15 for Paris. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone and party arrived at Biarritz at midnight on Wednesday. The right hon. gentleman appeared to be in excellent health. The Mayor of Liverpool has acceded to a requisition to call a meeting of the City Council to consider the pro- posal to confer the freedom of the city on Mr. Gladstone. At Accrington, on Tu3sday, a driver lost control over the engine of a goods train, and the train dashed into a warehouse, killing one man and injuring several others

"A year passed, and I had not seen her: We were ordered away, but before we went came a night upon which a great singer sang in opera. "It was one whose fame was world-wide. "I sat enraptured. div.head: ROE AND RINGLET
div.p: ROE AND RINGLET

Day was drawing to a close above the western horizon. The sunset's gold and purple clouds were heaped in gorgeous and fantastic forms. Long shadows lay upon the higher ground, and a purple mist filled the valley. From his low couch near the window of a crowded hospital, a wounded soldier looked out upon the scene, knowing well that he should never see the sun rise again—his doom was sealed. One of the most terrible of the battles of the Crimea had been fought, and that long, low place was crowded with the wounded and the dying— the dead also. The news of that battle would bring sorrow to many an English home. The face upon the pillow was bronzed and manly, yet almost regularly beautiful. The bright black hair, clustering about the temples, curled exquisitely. It was one a woman might love well, who lay there. So thought the comrade who bent over him, as the dying soldier's eyes turned upon him. "I have a favour to ask of you, Reginald," he said "When I am dead, place this packet upon my heart, and let no other ever see it. Open. it.' The officer whom he called Reginald obeyed. Within lay a rose, faded and withered long ago, and 41 long tress of golden hair, coiled up and tied with a blue ribbon. "Whose hair, Edward?" asked the young man The answer was a strange one. "I do not know." The young officer thought his friend's mind wan- dering; but the other looked up with a smile. "I do not know her name; but that is the hair of the woman I love—the only woman, Reginald. I saw her first when I was a child. I had gone into a little cave under a cliff I knew well, to seek shelter from the rain, and, looking up, saw what at first I thought was a fairy—a young child, as I knew in a moment, a girl so light and fair that she seemed almost unearthly. She was beautifully dressed, and her hair fell about her ahoulders. "'This is ray cave,' she said, 'but you may stay here, little boy.' "May ll' I said, laughing. come to be your cave?' "'Because I took it for mine,' she said. I hide here sometimes, and nurse searches for me every- where, but never' finds me. I shall never. let her find me. I like to know there is one place where I can do just as I like.' "Who are you?' I asked. "'I sha'nt tell you,' she said. "We stayed and talked for a long while; and, when the shower was over, she flitted away, and I did not know where she had gone. "I told my mother of her, but she knew no such child; and after that I used to find her in the cave very often. "I brought toys there, and dainties, and we grew very much like brother and sister. " I. used to ask her her name ; but she refused.to
'And how does it

give it. "You would begin to be respectful,' she said if you knew it.. I hate people to be respectful to me. I like to be just a litte girl. That's why I run away from nurse.' "This was all she would ever say, until at last our pleasant meetings came to an end. One day I found her looking very sad, and with traces of tears on her face. "I am going away, little boy,' she said, and I shall never see you again. I am going to give you this rose to remember me by, and a curl of my hair, and you must never forget me.' "I took the rose and the curl, folded in the very paper you held. there. 'But you must come back again,' I said. " I cannot,' she answered; but I shall love you always. Nice boy, kiss me.' Our little lips met. Now shut yo ux eyes until I say, Booh l' she cried. "I obeyed her,. but the cry did not come, and after an interval I opened them. She was no longer

"THE GEESE OFTHE'CILI,FELNVS." is- a highly-finished production. Its descriptive passages are splendidly written., and the interest with which the reader is filled even at the out- set 13-amply sustained to the end. It is full of highly-wrought dramatiesituations, and the local colouring with which it abounds is-admirable.. Sir Lancelot Callerley is a.magnifitent specimen of the English •gentleman, though his life is over- shadowed by the curse with which his family is burdened. His "child wife "—the Lady Sylvia—charms the follower of her career with her sweet nature, which can yet; flash into Indomitable courage on emergency, while- a, contrast is afforded • in tbe- fiery-spirited but malevolent Dorothy Breamish. Jack Breamish, whose chivalrous feelings towards Lady Callerley are capitally depicted, is a. likeable personage, while the many minor characters are all encel- ienty peurtrayed. The scenes o2scountry life and, the des- criptions of adventures by sea axe alike remarkably good, while some of the superstitions with . which the minds of evemiashionabie folk were imbued at the period covered, by the storyare graphic Ally sketched. Altogether the story Is well worthy of perusal,

div.head: EXECUTION AT SHEPTON. MALLET.
div.p: EXECUTION AT SHEPTON. MALLET.

-- Harry Dainton, thirty-five years of age, a mason, ot Bath, was executed at Snepton Mallet Goal, at eight o'clock on Tuesday morning, for the murder of his wife Hannah, by drowning her in the river Avon, at Bath, on September Bth. Billington, of Bolton, was 012 execu- tioner, and he allowed a drop of seven feet. Death was i vi instantaneous. The culprit made no allusion to the crime to the relatives who sited him. He spent 'rues- day afternoon writing to his relatives begging them to give up drink. He was attentive to the administrations of the chaplain, and acknowledged the justice of the sentence, but said he would confess to God, not to man. On the way to the scaffold he walked firmly, reiterating the words, ,‘ Oh! Lord Jesus, have mercy," and was uttering them in an exoited tone as the drop fell. The execution took place when the clock was striking eight, and the black flag was at once hoisted. About 500 people were outside the prison, The Press wa hat ad. mitted.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
FLOODING OF THE CANAL.-BANKS BURST AND
PLANT SUBMERGED.

For nearly a fortnight past, every possible precaution had been adopted by the canal authorities at various points from Irlam to Thelwall—points which were regarded as the weakest—to prevent another accident, but, unfortunately, these efforts have not been success- ful. The heavy fa 11 of snow and almost incessant rain, on Saturday caused the Mersey, which had dropped greatly, to rise again with great rap idity, until on Sun- day it reached a greater height than on the 11th inst. The greatest danger was at the memorable No. 5 cutt- ing on the Partington side of the river. This cutting which is three-quarters of a mile in length, is separated from the Mersey by two barriers. The lower barrier,how- ever, has to resist the united waters of the Irwell and Mersey, and moreover, is dangerously situated, because f the obstacles in the way for a free run of water. In the first place there is the railway bridge and the Stockport branch line, secondly there is a pile bridge in close prox- imity, over which the route line of the canal is carried, and the piles to a certain extent hold back the water. Thirdjy, the barrier is placed on the outer curve of a sharp turn in the course of the river. The sharpness of the turn can be well understood when a roller was re- quired to get the barges round in the days when the " Dukes " and "Barflies "traversed the river. Hence the barrier was opposed to the full rush and weight of water which last year literally burst thro ugh with a tremendous noise, and a wave of water quickly swept from one end of the cutting to the other. The barrier withstood the water, but notwithstanding all efforts, the cutting was invaded from the meadows near Peak Nook Farm. Here the water accumulated, but wasnot dangerous until the Mersey overflowed its banks in Carrington. This overflow joined the water previously in the meadows. The bank of the cutting was unable to withstand it, and with a loud noise the water burst through, dashing the bank to the other side, and pour- ing into the cutting in a broad sheet, which could be seen from a distance. To the workers on the canal this was a surprise, as they had only been made aware of the danger a short time previously, and though they endeavoured to strengthen the bank it was of no avail. There are now two large gaps in the bank varying from fifty to sixty yards. Several wagons were standing on the route line when the catastrophe occurred, and these were precipitated into the cutting, together with the rails. Cranes, wagons, navvies, and plant generally, were all submerged.

div.head: THELWALL.
div.p: THELWALL.

Great precautions were adopted all along the route of the canal, to prevent the water rushing into it, but at Thelwall all efforts proved unavailing. The weak point on the section, at least judging from events, was the embankment separating the old river (which at this point has been diverted) from the canal. A. good staff of workmen were employed throughout Sunday in strengthening the embankment, by various means, or the accident would not have been so long delayed. The river Bonin, however, swollen by the enormous quan- tity of water from the upper reaches, and the flooded meadows, continued rapidly to rise, and about eleven o'clock it was evident that nothing further could be done to resist the force of the water opposed to the embank- ment, the water not being able to escape in sufficient • volume by the syphon into the Mersey. Slowly at firs , water percolated through the embankment, and, at length, carrying everything before it, made a breach from 15 to 20 yards wide, and with a loud noise, spread itself along the bottom of the cutting to the right as far as it cm ',I go, namely, to the brickfields at Statham, where another embankment stretches across the Canal, and to the left as far as Morris Brook, near to the offices, where another embankment stopped it. Of course a large quantity of water rushed into the canal • every second, but its force soon abated, and it is said • that when it reached the embankment at Morris Brook it
• travelled very slowly indeed. The Thelwall cutting is now, therefore, flooded for about a mile and a half from 7 The embankment at Morris Brook to that near the brick-

- field at Statham. The depth of the water is estimated , at from 40 to 50 feet, and the cutting, except for its • great width,now presents the appearance of an ordinary • canal, scarcely a ripple to be seen upon it. There is no . probability of the water getting into the locks at Latch- ford, as the embankment at Morris Brook, already very • strong, has been further strengthened. • It is stated that no effort will be made to pump the -:•flood waters from the cuttings for same months. The •excavation, it is contended, has reached the full depth, . and the pressure of the water will keep the banks firm during the most critical period of the year. Next sum- , mer it will be an el.sy matter t 9 pump out the water and :give the proper pitching to the slopes.
A " LAKE " DISTRICT.
Owing_ to the heavy rdns, the river Bollin
-overflowe-d its banks and inundated the sur- roundina country for many miles. All the mea- •dows between Statham and Thelwali were one

vast expanse of water, with hardly a blade of ;grass to be seen as far as the eye could reach, the •view., only being relieved by a few solitary hedges. In 'Statham, the house of Mr. Thomas Brooks. cattle •dealer, was flooded, and the family suffered much incon- venience. Thelwall, however, suffered most from the inundation. Several of the roads, more particularly that leading past the Post Office, were flooded to a consider- able,clepth, and pedestrians in the habit of using these roads were compelled to make large circuits. The mischief, however, did not end here, for the lower apartments of many of the houses were flooded to a depth of several inches. In two cases so great was the depth of the water in the lower rooms that the tenants hadto remove the furniture to the higher apartments ; and at.a farm in the neighbourhood the cattle had to be removed ,from the shippons. It is reported that a num- ber.of•sheep were drowned on Sunday at Rizton. OFFICIAL REPJRT.

Ii their Official report of the recent floods„ the Ship Canal(Company say :—" The two cuttings at Partington and Thelwali have been filled owing to the flood water of the Mersey and Bollin breaking through the landown- ers' flood banks in several places and covering the meadows adjacent to the canal. The water gradually soaked into the light soil during Saturday and Sunday, and, the-rain • continuing, ultimately found its way into the cutting between Butchersfield and Morristown, causing :several landslips and damaging the embank- ments of the ovetland railway which form the flood dam on the sicte of the cutting. This is similar to what occur- red last year, but is much more limited in extent and is trifling in general comparison. The total tength of canal flooded last year visas aboyit 181 miles; this year it is about 21 males. The flooded cuttings were nearly finished and almost devoid of plant. The cuttings in which the Mode Wheel, Barton, Irlam, and Latchford locks are being constructed have escaped damage, so no delay wilt be caused in completing the works of the canal. The brickyard near Thelwall has also been flooded. No flood waters have gatinto the Pomona Docks,which have been gradually filling for the past fortnight. The heavy rains have caused art accumulation of water in some of the cuttings,but this forms no difficulty and will be pumped out in a few days:"

div.head: NEW EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE NEW EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE.

The new Exectaave Committee of representatives of the Board of Direttors of the Manchester Ship Canal and the City Council, the formation of which was announced on Saturday, has been made up of Sir E. J. Harwood, Mr. Alderman Chesters 'Thompson, Mr. Alderman Mark (ex- Mayor), and Mr. J. W. Southern on behalf of the Corpor- ation • and Mr. J. K. 'Bythell, Mr. S. R. Platt, and Mr. W. J. Crossley, as the three representatis-es of the share- holders. Sir John Harwood has been elected chairman. The committee met on Friday again, for two hours on Saturday, and they hati .a further gathering on Monday. Their business on each occasion was connected with making preparations forthe supply of materials required in the further progress of the Ship Canal works, to be submitted to public tender. In a day or so advertise- ments will be issued asking for tenders for coaj, stores of every description, and various kinds of material. Mr. G. H. Hill, C.E., the waterworks engineer for the Corpor- -ation, had intimated his desire to give up his connection with the Sbip Canal, but he has been induced to continue pesition as adviser to the Corporation,with additional -powers and safeguards vested in him on behalf of the -authority he represents. A NEW ASSOCIATECN OF SHAREHOLDERS. On Tuesday evening, a preliminary meeting of the Ship Canal shareholders was held at 63, King-st., Man- chester, to consider the formation of a shareholders' association. Mr. Reirben Spencer was voted to the chair. Mr. B. T. Belisha, who had publicly suggested the forma- tion of the association., said it was desired to form the association not to make money, but to protect the mutual interests of the shareholders, and possibly to secure for the shareholders such advantage as might be derived from the starting of any subordinate undertak- ings which might be originated in connection with the canal. The Chairman observed that they sere not there to make unpleasant comments on the actions of the directors. The Corporation held the key to the position in the circumstances which were known to them. It waB desirable to form the aesociation, not because there was immediate need for its action but for the protection of the shareholders in time of crisis. On the motion of Mr. Thomas Denbith, seconded by Mr. Thomas Jackson, It was resolved to form a committee of nine to carry put the objects of the meeting, with power to add to their number. The following gentlemen were nominated :-- Mr. Isaac David Belisha, Mr. John A. Beith, Mr. Reuben Spencer, County Alderman Forrest, Dr. William Arm- strong, air. James Oliver, Mr. Alfred Crewdson, Mr. George 'C. Haworth, and Mr. Hilton Greaves. The meeting closed with thanks to Mr. Belisha and the chair- man.

div.head: MILITARY TOURNAMENT ,AT THE
div.p: MILITARY TOURNAMENT ,AT THE
G YMN A MUM.

On Saturday evening a grand military tourna- ment was given by non-commissioned officers of the 12th Royal Lancers in the Warrington Gymn- asium. These was a numerous and select attend- ance. The first item consisted of dumb-bell exer- cise, after which a very picturesque performance consisting of lance exercise by a squad of the 12th Royal Lancers came off. The fine military appear- ance of those who took part, and the beautiful precision with which they went through their exercises excited much admiration. Exercises on the parallel bars, by leaders and members of the gymnasium,followed,after which there was a splen- did exhibition of sword exercise by a squad of Lan- cers. Barbells came afterwards, and then Sergeant-Major Bradley, assisted by Bombar- dier Bradley, 63rd battery, Colchester, performed in an inimitable manner, the following sword feats, which created the heartiest applause : Severing apple on hand blindfolded; severing apple in- side pocket handkerchief, without injuring the hand- chief ; severing broom handle suspended on two loops of paper held on the edges of two razors; slicing an apple under the heel of one of the audience withont touching the boot; cutting a shilling from under the heel of one of the audience without touching the boat. Sword versus sword was the next event—Troop Sergi.- Major Allen v. Private Reynolds, and Private G. Grant v. Private F. Grant being the performers. A rope climb- ing competition open to new members of the gymnasium only, the prize for which was a silver medal, succeeded, the successful climber being not ono of the most youthful of the competitors,but one of the more elderly,Dr. Kisby. The complete ascent of the rope a second time was, how- ever, a task none of them could achieve, though strenu- ous were the attempts made. in a ring competition, which followed, the first prize was a silver medal pre- sented by Dr. Kisby, and the second was also a silver medal. Mr. J. Podrnore was the winner of the first and Mr. J. Warren of the second. Fencing foils, which proved most diverting to the audience, through the re- sounding knocks which the combatants occasionally dealt on each other's well guarded sconces, formed the following event, T. S. M. Allen, being pitted against ' Private Reynolds, and Private G. Grant against Private F. Grant. More sword feats by Sergeant Major Brad- ley assisted by the Bombardier, then came, these being announced on the programme as follows : Extinguishing lighted candle with edge of sabre ; Sir Charles Napier's great Indian feat—cutting the string of a suspended apple, and then the apple before it reaches the floor ; severing an ordinary broom-handle resting on the inner edges of two glasses of water, without spilling the water; severing an apple resting on the glass of a watch without injuring the watch. All these announce- ments were most expertly and cleverly carried out, except the last, the glass, as the Sergeant-Major can- didly informed his audience, who might else, indeed, for the most part have failed to realise the fact, having been broken. A succeeding boxing competition be- tween Privates G. and F. Grant, credited considerable interest and amusement. A performance with Indian clubs by leaders and members of the gymnasium closed the programme, but a few extra performances were given by the members of the institution. We may mention that Mr. E. Alexander acted as director of the proceedings, and Mr. T. R. Ford, as accompanist.

div.head: WA.RUNGTON SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: WA.RUNGTON SAVINGS BANK.

The anual meeting of the trustees and managers of this bank, was held at the Bank Premises, Buttermaket-street, on Tuesday morning. Major Pickmere presided, and there were also present, Alderman Holmes, Alderman Harrison, Alderman Francomb, Revs. J. Yonge, F.K.Freeston, F. W. Willis ; Councillor J. H. Fleming, Messrs. F. Monks, R. Garnett, G. Owen, W. Owen, H. N. Houghton, J. Geddes, J. R. Young, W. Long; and J. E. Davies (actuary).

The above plainly shows that the Government had in hand on account of this bank more than would pay the depositors the amount due to them, and that with the amount in the treasurer's hand there is the large sur- plus of £2,993 4s. id. The business of the bank steadily increases, the number of transactions during the year being 171,558: in 1881, they numbered 14,252. The total number of depositors now i 510,709 with £295,747 17s. sd. to their credit ; in 1871 the depositors numbered 3,780 with £271,371 ss. 3d. to their credit. The Sav- ings Bank Act, 1891, is now in 'force and new rules are being prepared in conformity with the Act and as soon as they are passed and printed they will b 3 issued to depositors on their attendance at the bank. Ths CHAIRMAN moved that the statement of accounts prepared by the actuary and examined by the account- ant be approved ; that copies be transmitted to the National Debt Commissioners and to the Inspector ap- pointed under the 1891 Act, and that a duplicate be publicly affixed in the Savings Bank.—Mr. W. Lowu seconded the proposal.—Councillor FLEMING said that the value of those buildings were not credited in the balance sheet; to whom did they belong ?—Mr. Daryies said the buildings were their own, and besides the money balance they had got the buildings as well.—The motion was then agreed to.

div.head: kiECTION OF OFFICERS.

The following. officers were appointed :—Chairman, Major Pickinere vice-chairman, Mr. W. Long; COM- mittee of Management, the Chairman, vice-chairmatx ; Revs. J. Yonge, and F. K. Freeston ; Messrs. C. -J. Holmes, F. Monks, R. Garnett, Joseph Davies, J. Geddes, G. Dakin, R. W. Francomh, W. Darbyshire, J. R. Young, T. Sutton, H. N. Houghton, J. Harrison, and W. Owen.

div.head: NEW RULES
div.p: NEW RULES

The CHAIRMAN said they would have to arrange new rules in accordance with the new Act of Parliament and they should now have an inspector. 'rho new rules would have to be deposited in the Bank for 28 days, and be open to the public, and if nobody objected to them they should have a special meeting to pass them. Votes of thanks to the Chairman and Committee of Management were also passed.

div.head: WESLEYAN MISSIONARY MEETING.
div.p: WESLEYAN MISSIONARY MEETING.

On Monday evening the annual meetiag in con- nection with the Wesleyan foreign missions, was held at the Wesleyan Chapel, Bewsey-road, Warring- ton. Mr. Councillor Beaman presided. There was a good attendance, considing the wetness of the night. The Chairman and the Rev. Thomas Ross having made some remarks, the Rev. A. Freeman read the last annual report as to the progress of foreign missions, which showed a deficit, on the year, of over £lO,OOO, and a total deficit, with that of prev- ious years, of £19,377. The receipts from the Warrington circuit had been £212 15s. 4d. The report was generally of a most favourable character. —The Chairman subsequently addressed the meeting. He thought the report was full of hope, and promise aid encouragement. Although perhaps some might say that I missionary labour was very speculative he failed to see it. It might not rouse the enthusiasm that it formorly did, but he believed it was laid deep down in our affections. India in the report held the premier position, and very rightly too. It was • a mighty empire. but Hinduism was a much mightier system, containing within itself so many:apparently incongruous elements derived from very different sources and introduced at very different periods yet forming now one mighty whole. To the Hindoo every act of daily life was fraught with seine religious meaning. When wespoke of Hindooism we did not mean religion in the narrow sense understood in this country. Hindooism had solved, as no other system had yet solved, the problem that lay before our own church in our own day, the prob.- lei of making every act of life in the highest sense an act of worship. As to China in the present excited state of the public mind consequent upon the horrible atroeities against, and massacres of Christians there, he felt he could not trust himself to speak, but let these not Inflame their passions but rather stimulate their sympa- thies towards the benighted people of that unhappy land. Africa had ever been an important field of mission work, and this was being more and more advanced there by the unprecedently rapid progress of geographical discovery within the past few years. The Revs. Thos. Ross and A. Freeman having spoken, the Rev. James Lewis, of Eccles, succeeded. He said the progress of missionary work had been inconceivably rapid, and had a man 100 years ago predicted the results of foreign , missions, men would have cried out in the utmost deri- sion and scorn behold the dreamer comes. fle quoted the opinion of Lord Lawrence that Christian missions had done more for India than all other agencies, and the ; remark of Max Muller that India \ was already saturated from end to end with Christian sentiment. He also quoted the" Times " to show that Christianity in India was increasing, while Hinduism was decreasing. Some people said the heathen had their religion and if they lived up to their light they would be accepted of God. But if a man lived up to his light as many of the heathen did, did he not deserve more light? It was not a ques- tion so much of whether the heathen should be saved if they did not accept the gospel as whether we should be saved if we did not send it.—On the motion of the Rev.

MILLS'S DICK.

When owd Stamp Duty wur abeawt, An' Stitch-V-Time wur wick, Ther lived a reg'lar rooter here— Thay caw'd him Mills's Dick. He uset to train fer th' Grand Owd Mon— Eatar Grand Owd Mon—named Stone; " k fine owd English gentleman," Wo wur ekcell'd hi noan. To hear King Dick sort up his dogs, Virtu deawnreet fun galore; They watch't him just like Christians, 'cose He very seldom swore He'd say, "Lie deawn, thee, Satirist, An' thee, Sea Pilot, too' • Poor Spie-an'-Spon's like Bonypart--- Hoo's lost a Wayterloo I" " Neaw, Sterrup Cup, wot's up wi thee? Wot makes thi yelp an' skirl? Art wantin' t' give a ugly snap At poor owd Strawberry Girl ?" An' so, wi' ey'ry dog i'th' pack, His time an' skill wur spent; Till one fine morninr off he sect To Burton-upo'-Trent. Neaw he's amung the busy B's That's own'd bi Mester Bass; Aw know he'll alias do his best To loud his naester's brass. Its not lung sin' he welly won A rattlin' stake or two; But he cudn't fill his Budget quite, Wi' larkin' at Belle Vue. Wi' Spree Boy and the Bogie Mon He roams the fields an' woods; Wile Blackcock's kept i' Bondage wi' His fav'rite Bridget's Buds! (Poor Buds !—Aw've heerd Dick sigh an' say, He'd bowt fro scores o' studs; But for bein' willin', wick, an' gam', Jle nair bed one like Buds!) In summer time, he duz a bit 0' gardenia' fer fun; An' mony a prize wi' cabbitches An' collyfleawrs he's won. One cabbitch grow'd so awful big-- It's true, wot aw relate— Thay cudn't get it eawt to th' show, Till they'd shifted th' garden gate At anny rate, Dick towd uz so, An' swore hi Holy Writ, That it wur fact; but mebbe he Wur stretchin' it a bit.

Sumtimes he wet to goo an' fish, An' once he hookt a treawt, That wur so big, he broke his arm Wi' pooin' th' beggar eawt ! An' wot a promiser he wur ! But sometimes he'd forget ; He promis't me a pup lung sin', But it hasn't rowt mi yet! An' eh! the hares aw shud have had, It puzzles mi to tell; By Gyow ! aw sumtimes wunder if He eyts um aw hissel ! Nair mind, owd lad, of aw the breed 0' trainers theawet the boss; An' fer a gradely mank or spree, There's mony a theausand woss. So. when theau runs thi final coorse, No matter slow or quick, Aw hope theaul spin reet slick away, If they slip thi wi Owd Nick I TUM 0' PEGS. Nyowton, God bless o'. December, 1891.
MYSTERIOUS AFEAIR. THREE PERSONS FOUND DEAD.

John Leahy, his wife, and their little grandson, were found dead on Thursday morning in one bed, at a lodg- ing-house in Bantry. They all appeared in good health when they went to bed. When Leahy's daughter, who lodges in an adjoining house, went to call her father to go to work. she found them dead. A tin vessel contain- ing tea was on a table beside the bed. It is supposed that death resulted from poison, and a post-mortem examination will be held.

TRAGEDY IN CHESHIRE.
A LABOURER SHOT.

William Royle, farmer, Hollia Edge Farm, Northern Etchells. near Cheadle, Cheshire, is in custody of the police on the charge of causing the death of one of his labourers on Tuesday night. It seems that the labour- ers on Tuesday night. It seems that the labourer in question, whose name is Beech, and who came from Blackburn, was sent to the post office with a letter. He returned about 8.30, and for some time jokes passed between him, his master, and another man named Joseph Wright with respect to Beech's unshaven appearance. The joking proceeded, and Wright and Royle placed Beech on a chair and attempted to shave him with an old knife. Beech retaliated, and said he had firearms In his possession. Royle said, "Oh, have you? So have I,' and immediately took a gun from the kitchen ceiling, pointed it at the head of Beech, and fired, the result being that Beech's brains were blown out, and he died without a groan. Hoyle was at once taken into custody by Policeman Massey. His explanation of the affair is that it was all a joke, and he did not know that the gun was loaded. Deceased, who has been in the employment of Royle and his family for a period of 14 years, was on the best of terms with his master up to the time of the occurrence.
Royle was brought up at a special sitting of the Stock- port Polic3 Court on Wednesday, and after some evid- ence had been given, was remanded on bail till I uesday.
THE It ikIT.WAY FATALITY AT THE VULCAN.
THE SPECIAL JURY'S VERDICT REVERSED BY
THE JUDGE.

At Thursday's sitting of the Liverpool Assizes, it may be remembered, the special jury sworn in this case gave their verdict for the plaintiffs, damages £l5O and costs. The action had been brought by Mrs. Elizabeth Holcroft, on account of the loss of her husband, a toolsmith, at the Vulcan Ironworks, Newton-le-Willows, who had met his death on the morning of June 9th, in crossing the London and North-Western Railway Company's line after breakfast. The jury's verdict had been given at the close of the eourt, and after counsel had left. On Friday Mr. Gully, Q.C. M.P., calling attention to remarks in his iorcterlip's summing up of the case, asked that judgment be given for the defendants. His Lordship said that if he were obliged to give his opinion, he was bound to give it irrespective of convenience or consequences. He had the greatest possible respect for the opinion of the jury, but he thought the case had not been made out for the plantiff as a matter of law. The first point was whether there was any evidence of negligence on the Ipart of the defendant company. By the plaintiff's story, the deceased had been in the habit of using the line for many years, and if the opening of the crossing gate was a trap for people not accustomed to the line, it could not be a trap for a man who must have known that it was no indication of there being no danger on the line, and it did not convoy any invitation to him to cross. Even one of the workmen who had crossed immediately before , the deceased attempted it, had seen the train approach- ing. He was clearly of opinion that the plaintiff had ' failed to connect negligence, if any, with the defendant company, and judgment ought therefore to be given for the defendants. Mr. Gully.—With costs? His Lord- ship.—Yes.—Mr. Kennedy.—Your lordship will grant us a stay? Mr. Gully.—We won't be in a hurry about the costs.

div.head: PEOPLE'S COLLEGE CONCERT.
div.p: PEOPLE'S COLLEGE CONCERT.

The annual concert in connection with the People's College was held on Thursday evening in the Public Hall, Warrington. As on previous occa- sions there was a crowded attendance. Mr. W. Long presided. The entertainment consisted of a rendering by the scholars of the cantata "Life at Sea" the music of which had been composed by Mr. T. Mee Pattison who was at one time a scholar at the People's College and who was also the organist on Thursday evening. The cantata is excellently adapted for a performance of this kind, and certainly the highest praise is due for the manner in which it was interpreted by the scholars. Besides the more active performers there were- accommodated on the platform a chorus of over 300 children, and these all being prettily attired added much to the attractiveness of the s
costumes and "get-up "of the performers, blackest of black savages with spears, to th( telling sailors, were all well suited to the char parts. _ In the course of the play many solos

and trios were sung, and in nearly every inE youthful artists, acquitted themselves in unexceptionable fashion. The singers of solo • F. Clarke, H. Gibbon, A. Parkinson, C. Jca Dyke, T. Aukland, and G. Smith; duets wer • H. Houghton. and H. Gibbon, G. Smith, and E ton, and trios by A. Tilling,J W. Dyke, and H ton. In the second part the song of the gipsh the tambourine on high "won a round of applause, and G. Smith's song "A tar of the Qa._ • was warmly encored. The singing indeed as awhole of the highest order, and reflected the great, t cri upon the conductor, the Rev. E. Moore. During an interval, the CHAIRMAN said he t.it granted that a large number of the audiem strong and personal interest in the proceeding: r evening, and, more than that, that they also too g; interest in the success, and the details of that sr ,:s=

the People's College, and therefore before mal g any further remarks he would call upon Mr. J. J. c cfiela to read the report of the managers. Mr. J. J. CROSFIELD then read the report as f . —This school has had another prosperous year no 'Eh- standing a considerable amount of sickness during the months of March, April, and May, the time of the in- fluenza. epidemic. With this drawback the attendance showed an increase on that of the former year and the average for the past three months is higher by over 30 than at any previous time. The average attendance for the year ending September 30th was 758, and the number of children examined in the various standards 897. Of these 419 were examined in standards one, two or three, and of the remainder, 167 were examined in standards four, 148 in standard five 111 in standard six, and 52 in standard seven. It will be seen from these numbers that 478, or considerably more than half the scholars, were examined in standards four and upwards, standards which make the greatest demand upon the efforts and powers of the teachers. It may be added that not less than 1,300 scholars had been under instruc- tion during tie year in the People's College, and the branch infants' schools connected with it in Cairo-street and at Bank Quay. As the result of the examination by her Majesty's Inspector, the school has again been awarded the highest possible grants for the elementary subjects, reading, writing, and arithmetic; for the class subjects, English. geography,needlework, and singing, and also for discipline and organisation. In the specific subjects 86 boys passed in one or other of the three stages of algebra, 78 girls in one or other of the three stages of domestic economy, and 28 boys of standard 7 in the first stage of shorthand. The results of the cookery classes were most encouraging, and it is satis- factory to know that many parents have appreciated the training their daughters had received. For the first time for some years all the girls were examined in draw- ing on the same terms as the boys, and the highest mark —excellent, was gained throughout. This was a most Igratifying feature, as the children examined in the various drawing standards numbered 900. Minnie Butterworth, Clara S. Dinwiddie, and Isaac Bowen 'whose terms of apprenticeship as pupil teachers ended in September each obtained Queen's scholarships of the first class, at the annual examination of pupil teachers for admission to Training Colleges in July last. As you are aware the Committee accepted the fee grant provided by the new Education Act of this year, and were thus enabled to make a considerable reduction in the fees from the Ist October last. It is impossible to say what will be the result of the new arrangement yet, ERA confidence is felt that the outcome will be satisfactory all round if parents will support the managers and teachers by insist- upon their children attending regularly throughout the year. The Committee have only to add that they have I decided to increase the staff by two additional mistresses to make tha teaching still more thoroughly efficient. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN said he would emphasize to some small extent some passages in the report. He thought that, in the first place, they must congratulate not only the managers of the school and the teaching staff, but also the town of Warrington itself on the continued success of the school. He thought that when they looked around them and saw the great work that was being done in Warrington in the education of their young people they could not but be gratified at the success of each and all of them ; but more than that he claimed for the People's College an increased amount of sympathy on the part of the public in that it was thoroughly and entirely unsectarian. (Hear, hear.) All children who came to that school were treated as in every sense equal, and it depended on their own merits as to how far they got. (Hear, hear.) One passage in the report spoke of the adoption of the fee grant which had enabled the managers to reduce the fees of the school, and he should like to use a vulgar expression, to "rub in" upon the minds of the parents of the children those remarks, which pointed to the necessity of their help in promothao• the regular attendance of their children. It was in °that way they could help forward the success of the school and at the same time permanently benefit their children. They had heard of the increase of the staff, and that went to show that no effort would be spared on the part of the managers to increase the efficiency and the success of the work done. (Hear, hear.) Whilst they were at that stage of the evening he should say how much indented the school was for the admirable effici- ency of the children in their musical attainments to the 'Rev. E. Moore as teacher of the school. (Applause.) He mentioned Mr. Moore more particularly in connection with that entertainment. The merits of the rest of the teaching staff was,he thought,sufficiently spoken to bythe -success they had had in the Government grant. (Hear. 'hear.) He should like on their behalf, and on behalf of severybody concerned,to thank their old friend,Mr. Patti- son, for the way in which he conducted his share of the work. (Applause.) Mr. Pattison was an old scholar of that school of which no doubt he was, proud, and it was an.evidence of his continued interest in it that he came down there all the way from London to conduct those concerts. (Applause.) He was sure they would award Mr. Pattison hearty thanks, and also to the headmaster

div.head: SHOCKING COLLIERY FATALITY.
div.p: THE SHOCKING COLLIERY FATALITY.

"PRETTY STIFF LYING." The inquest on the body of Thomas Marsh, 16 years of age son of Henry Marsh, 70, Brook-street, who was killed by a fall of roof in the No. 11 pit of the St. Helens Collieries Company, on the 7th inst., was resumed before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the Town Hall, on Tuesday forenoon. At the opening of the inquest last week it was stated that the deceased worked as a drawer for his father and brother, who were colliers. The evidence showed that the place had not been sufficiently" propped," and the father and son stated that they could not put up more props, as none were to be found at the proper place where they had to be left by the officials of the mine. It was also said that it was the duty of the colliers to make their working places safe by sufficient propping, and that the proprie- tors were bound to store props for that purpose at stated places. The inquiry was adjourned until Tuesday for the attendance of Mr. H. Hall, the Government inspector Mr. Hall was present at the resumption and Mr. J. 0 Swift represented the colliery proprietors ; Mr. J. P. Mearns appeared for the relatives of the deceased, and Mr. T. Glover attended as the miners' agent. The evi- dence given ma the former occasion was rePeated,and the Coroner explained that the question was whether the employers, as they were bound to by the Act, had pro- vided a sufficient number of props for the men.—Thomas Bradbury, underground manager, deposed that on Friday preceding the Monday on which the accident occured he saw sufficient props in the " shunt," the appointed place where they were to be kept, to last over Monday or Tuesday. Re saw some props there shortly after the accident.—Samuel Walker, a day-wage man, said he was working near the Marsh's at the time of the accldent. He sa.w props alongside the roof and in the "shunt."— Thomas Brannan, the shotlighter, gave corroborative evidence, and Thomas Topping, who was called by Mr. Mearns gave similar testimony.—Joseph Johnson, a pony driver, said he did not take particular notice on the morning of the accident whether or not there were any props in the " shunt."—At this stage the Coroner said he had other inquests to attend at Liverpool, and he must again adjourn if the inquiry was likely to con- tinue some time.—Mr. Swift said he had a lot of wit- nesses to call, unless the jury were prepared to say they had heard sufficient evidence and were agreed on a simple verdict of" accidental death."—The Coroner re- marked that that there were discrepancies in the evid- ence, and it was evident that,one way or the otherithere had been a good deal of pretty stiff lying going on. It was for the jury to consider on which side the blame rested.—Mr. Swift: If the jury are going to blame the Company for the accident I must call my other witnesses. —The Coroner said he did not want to be called on to decide upon the conflicting evidence.—The Foreman, after consulting with several jurors, said : I don't think, , as far as the evidence has gone, that we can say it was a purely accidental death.—lt was then arranged that the inquiry should be adjourned until Thursday. The inquiry was resumed on Thursday and several more wit- nesses were examined. It took the jury about twenty minutes to consider their verdict. The foreman (Mr. J. H. Houghton) said they had arrived at a verdict of " Accidental death," but they thought tha firemen in charge from Saturday to Monday had neglected their duty in not seeing that the place was properly timbered, i and they alai thought that there was a scarcity of suit- able timber.

A train from Hastings, due at East Croydon at 8.54 on Thursday morning ran into the rear of a special train containing lads from Ardingley College on their way to London, at Selhurst Junction. Several lads sus- tained cuts and bruises, while both the up and down lines were temporarily blocked. The accident was due to fog.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

Mr. J. Mclntyre presiderl over the fortnightly meeting 11.4 d at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present—Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Parr, Lewis, W.Whitlow, R. Wade, Aaron, Brandreth, J: Whitlow, Turner, Knowles, H. Whitlow, Heywood, J. Stokes, Edwards, J. Baguley, P. Hall, Pickering,Bretherton, John Weir, C. Reynolds, J.P. (ex-officio), Smith, J. Ashton, (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk).
HELSBY SEWERAGE.

A letter was read from Mr. S. Thorneley, solicitor, Chelsea, asking what the Authority had decided to do with regard to the sewers on Mr. Thorneley's property at Helsby, and also with regard to providing a proper sewerage scheme for disposing of the sewage of the town- ship.—The Clerk said he had replied that the Committee had not finally reported ou the matter.
THE SHIP CANAL.

Tbe Clerk said he had received notice from the Ship. Canal Company of their intention to apply at the next Parliament for a Bill to do certain works, and the sewers of Runcorn, Frodsham, and West3n were set out.—lt was resolved that the Clerk reply that the Board dis- sented from the proposal, and also to procure a copy of th bill.
TEACHING THE BOARD THEIR DUTY.

The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Joseph Pritchard, watchmaker, Runcorn, with reference to the Halton Brook Ditch Drain as follows :—I am very greatly sur- prised by the contents of the letter of your inspector of nuisances dated the Bth inst. Now if you are what you profess to be "The Sanitary Authority " for this district and are empowered as you profess to be by the Public Health Act, why do you not act as men who know their position and are determined to do their duty. If it is your duty to cover in the sewers of the district, then do your duty and not try to place your duty on other people's shoulders. And if it is not your duty to do it, then it becomes your duty to see that those whose duty it is to do it, do:their duty, and not to whine like a child because it will cost the township somewhere about a farthing in the £on the rates. It appears to me you want waking up—(laughter)—to a sense of your duty and I am much of opinion that the best way for me to proceed would be to apply for an injunction to prevent you from using this drain as a sewer at all and so compelling you to make a sewer in the public road, and then we would see whether you would whine at the payment of is. in the £ instead of fd. The Committee you appointed as a deputation to consult with me on the subject would neither tell me what they thought nor what they intended to propose and therefore your Inspector's letter was a surprise, in that I consider it added insult to injury for I consider that yonr action in attempting to convert that which from its very nature could have only been intended as a surface drain into a common sewer, inflicts upon me a very great injury as it prevents me from using to its fullest extent my freehold or in other words, you virtually rob me of over fifty yards of my land. This I do not feel inclined ,to sit down to quietly for you are the Authority and therefore must know :—First, that under the Public Health Act I cannot be compelled to accept through my , freehold the sewerage of the eight houses which have I recently been erected; secondly, your being the author- ity of the district it is your duty under the Public Health Act to provide an outfall for the sewerage of the said houses; thirdly, as provided by the same Act you know that such outfall can only be made by you on the Queen's highway or upon land which has been purchased by the Board for the purpose.—Fourthly, you know that the cost of such outfall must be paid out of the rates and that each ratepayer must be called upon to pay his proportion according to his rateable value. Now looking to the fact that such outfall would cost the township over £lOO and further looking to the fact that the rateable value of the property in the immediate neighbourhood is very little. lam willing to meet the Authority on condition that you pay me an acknow- ledgment for the use of the drain through my land and so save any great expense until the neighbourhood be- comes more thickly populated and a proper system of sewerage is adopted by the district.—Mr. Baguley said the sub-committee which was dealing with this matter had asked Mr. Pritchard if he would contribute a trifle if the Authority piped the ditch and he replied that he would if the other owners would. There were four or five interested.—The Nuisance Inspector said his letter was simply to the same effect. For generations drainage had gone into that ditch, and it belonged to the Authority without a doubt.—Mr. Stokes described the circumstances of the case, and asked if there was anything to prevent the Authority carrying out the Committee's decision to put in a pipe and connect it with the drain.—The Clerk replied no, and the Chairman said if the ditch was a public sewer they could drain into it any quantity of new houses.—The Inspector said asking for a small contribution had given rise to that letter.— Mr. Thos. Wright, of Halton, had written with reference to the same matter that he should be pleased to contri- bute a moderate and reasonable amount towards the expenses so as to relieve the rates of the township. He should also be pleased to improve the private drainage at the proper time--The letter was referred to the sub- committee on the motion of Mr. Aaron, who was added to the Committee. THE WATER SUPPLY AT PRESTON 'OTH HILL.
Mr. Aaron directed attention to the water supply at Preston 'oth' Hill, and the Inspector was instructed to make full inquiries and report.
THE RIVERS POLLUTION ACT.

The Inspector said he had made a complete investi- gation as to the pollution of the Mersey in that district, and he found that there was practically no sewage turned into the river from that Union. Most of the sewage was turned into the river by Lancashire towns.

div.head: KECKWICK BROOK
div.p: KECKWICK BROOK

The Inspector produced four analyses in each of which it was stated that the water was very poisonous, and highly charged with sulphuretted hydrogen. An analysis of Freston Brook described that stream as pretty strong sewage.—Mr. W. Whitlow said there could not be much sewage or the fish would not live in it as they did—Mr. Aaron said Mr. Earp had stated that he tanned with vat t brook and used no chemicals, but sometime previously he had stated that he had a chemical process of his own He (Mr. Aaron) said Mr. Earn was not wholly to blame for the pollution of the brook ; Aston Estate were also offenders. A long private discussion took place, but no decision was arrived at with regard to the legal proceed- ings against Mr. Earp, sanctioned by the Local., Govern- ment Board.

div.head: SEWERAGE OF STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: THE SEWERAGE OF STOCKTON HEATH.

The NuiWan-cf-irin-s-P-ea-o;-re-p-o-riai-that the Stockton Heath Sewerage Extension Committee had considered the memorial in reference to the provision and extension of the main sewerage at Stockton Heath. The Commit- tee were unanimously of opinion that a main sewer is required in what is known as the New Road, there being no proper drainage for the property already erected thereon.—The Inspector explained that in order to pro- vide a sewer for the road in question it would be neces- sary to obtain another sewer outfall at the lower end of the village of Walton Inferior' and that when the syphon at present being constructed under the Ship Canal at Twenty Step Bridge was completed it would be neces- sary to take up the sewer from such bridge to Wilders- pool as the existing sewer would be insufficient to take the whole of the sewerage from Stockton Heath to the present outfall. He also said that the sewer in Chester- road was in a very defective condition and would have to be taken up and improved. It was finally agreed that Mr. Percy Silcock be instructed to prepare an inexpen- sive tracing of the plan laid down by the Inspector, and submit the same to an adjourned meeting.—The report was approved.

WONES IRISH LEAGUE AND THE —LOCAL BOARD APPOINTMENTS. The usual weekly meeting of the abovelLeague was held on Sunday afternoon, under the presidency of Dr. O'Keeffe. A discussion took place with regard to the elections of the Widnes Local Board. Mr. Whelan and Mr. O'Connor strongly condemned the method by which certain persons were appointed to fill the vacancies. Mr. O'Connor proposed, and Mr. McMahon seconded the following resolution :—" Re- solved, that we hereby strongly protest against the method by which the vacancies on the Widnes Local Board have been filled, and we also strongly condemn the action of certain persons in the. town in trying to introduce religious influence into parliamentary, municipal, and other elections."—The Chairman, putting the resolution to the meeting, said he entirely agreed with it. The method by which certain parties in the town used their influence in the recent elections was simply absurd. He had no part in it, nor was he consulted in the matter at all. He considered it an insult to them as an organiza- tion, and one of the oldest in the town, not to be con- sulted on matters which affected them as Irishmen, and their interest in the management of the town. He asked them to unite, in order that they might show their power when the time came, by placing men in public positions who would have the entire confidence of the League. The resolution was passed unanimously.

Fire on Wednesday morning completely destroyed the Salvation Army barracks at Southport, a large building originally erected as an engineering works. The death is announced of the Dowager Lady de Ros, which took place on Wednesday at Eaton-place, Lon- don. Lady de Ros was a daughter of the fourth Duke of Richmond, and was born in 1795. General Booth, on leaving Ceylon, where he remains a week, goes to Madras, where he will stay four days. On Bth January he reaches Calcutta,and goes to Bombay on 16th January, leaving on the 21st. Yellow fever is reported to be raging with epidemic virulence at Santos, hundreds of persons dying daily. The " New York Herald "adds that the mortality among the crews of ships is awful.

BILLIARDS AND WHIST TOURNAMENT.—The following is the result of the first games in a billiard and whist tournament, which has just been played between the members of the Golborne and Ashton Conservative Clubs at Ashton, and which resulted in a win for the Ashton team on both games :—Billiards: Ashton 937, Golborne 853. At whist, the totals were Ashton 118, Golborne 80.
