SIDNEY WEBB on giving evidence on Town Hold- ings mentioned a case of land in Kensington which if sold and utilised for building purposes would be rated at from £15,000 to £lB,OOO per year. The actual rating was £62 only! There would be an end of such anomalies if land values were taxed as they ought to be. And so with agricultural land which is allowed to be idle. The landlord should be made to realise that the tax must be paid whether the land brings in anything or nothing. This would mean that he would have to sell if he was short of capital to work the whole of his land—and a very good thing too in many cases. There are thousands of acres in this coun- try which are producing nothing, or next to nothing, simply because the noble owner is in such an ignoble position that he cannot live in costly style and at the same time spend money on his estate. A tax on the land value, if it were sufficiently large, would force him to sell; and the land, by one person or another, would be cultivated as it ought to be. The same principle would apply to land encriched by minerals; the tax upon the value would break in upon that in- nate selfishness which enables the landowners of this country to appropriate millions of money annually in the shape of mine rents,way leaves, and royalties—money not a penny of which they can be said to have earned. The Financial Reform Asso- ciation is doing good work in directing attention to these matters; an in issuing year by year an almanac which is an unrivalled storehouse of statistics upon these and other matters of national importance.

As the worst use you can put a Spend And Save.4 man to is to shoot him, so the best use you can put the man of the future to is to educate him as the boy of to - day. Every polind spent locally or nationally in education is more than a pound saved. This is difficult of belief to those who cannot see the good of "book learning " ; but it is true, nevertheless ; and Mr. BRUNNER, M.P., was engaged at Sand- bitch, on Monday, in demonstrating its truth. It is well known that, having regard to the increpe of population, there has been a large diminution of crime and pauperism, and it is not disputed that this is duo almost entirely to the national advance in education. But it may still be asked—ls the improvement worth the money? The answer is not orly Yes, but that the expenditure in educa- tion is a positive gain. Mr. BRUNNER'S estimate is that we are spending in this country, including free libraries, about £7,000,000 annually en edu- cation; but as against thishe has the authority of Sir JOHN LUBBOCK for saying that, if the cost of paupers and criminals had gone on increasing with the increase of population, we should have been spending £10,000,000 more than we are to-day; in other words, the expenditure of £7,000,000 on education is an actual saving of £3,000,000 a year. This as to the financial, but what as to the moral, , aspect of the case? This is how it is viewed by ' the member for the Northwich Division: "They had, unfortunately, in the prisons of Great Britain and Ireland to-day some 13,000 unhappy people. But if crime had increased proportionately to the increase of population, they would have had 36,000 instead of 13,000, so that they had been spending £7,000,000 a year in rescuing 23,000 people from a life of misery and crime?' In view of such a result, Mr. BRUNNER sets a wise example in spending, and encouraging others to spend, in the direction of education. He has promised the people of Sandbach financial aid if they adopt the Free Libraries Act, and the Technical Instruction Act, and they will do well to accept his liberal offer. Working-men who may hesitate about taxing them- aeives should remember that they can have no bet- ter weapon for protecting themselves than educa- tion, and the organisation which almost invariably comes of it. They have nothing to lose, but every- thing to gain by helping themselves in this way. It is satisfactory to observe that an advance is being made at Widnes. It was decided at a meet- ing of the School Board, on Tuesday, "That on and after the Ist January next no school fees shall be charged in any of the infant schools under the Board." This means Free Education out-and-out in the numerous Board Schools of Widnes ; and it will soon be succeeded, in all pro- bability, by the adoption of a similar policy in Voluntary Schools. When will Warrington and St. Helens be in a position to follow suit ? They are not even alive as yet to the advantages of a School Boaid.

BEFORE the next issue of this Christmas journal another Christmas Day Greeting. will have come and gone, and we shall be near the close of the year. In accordance with custom at this period, we present each of our readers with an Illustrated Sheet Almanac, and we wish them "A Merry. Christmas," whilst pro- viding a few columns of reading with the object of helping to make it merry. The weather hitherto has not been very sea:sonable ; but it may change in the sleep of , a night, if not in the twinkling of an eye, and we may awake any morning to find such a transformation scene, with snow on the ground, as Dame Nature alone can make. That will be delightful to the young who are well-fed and well-clad; but it should never be forgotten that a fall of the temperature means "hard times" to thousands who are, insufficiently provided with food, fuel, and clothing; and, further, that severe cold is an active agent in thinning the ranks of aged people. It fortunately happens that trade this year, taking, the country through, is fairly good. The great bulk of people are in a position to thoroughly enjoy the good cheer of the season, and to heighten their enjoyment by stretching a helping hand to those Who are less favourably situated. It is to the credit of the toiling classes, in all towns and in all countries, that they have ever been ready to share the good things of life with those about them. It is a hard world as it is, but it would be very much harder to many if it were not that the poor are so considerate of each other, and so helpful to each other. It is not that those above them lack sympathy so much as they lack knowledge as to where help should be given, and how it should be given. This was not so "in the olden time" when the master worked and lived nmongst his men. We have changed all this with our huge factoriesand forges; and the long unlovely streets for the workpeople, while the employer lives in a villa some miles away. We have gained power of production by the change, but we have iost power of sympathy; and this is never more 'evident than when men come to take stock of each other, as they do at the re-proclamation of the ever old and ever new message of "peace on earth, good-will to men." There is a time for all things, and immemorial custom has determilhed that Christmas-tide is the time for— Jest, and youthful jollity, Quips and cranks, and wanton wiles, Nods and becks, and wreathed smiles.
Whatever the elders may think: and feel, after pursuing and seeing burst so many beautiful

bubbles, the young can at least enjoy themselves right heartily, if the opportunity be given them ; and it should be given as far as means will afford, for the young are young but once in a life-time. Happily,civilisation has brought one compensation in the shape of good things—things as cheap and beautiful as they are good—for the mind as well as the body; and they are indeed poor who cannot gratify " the.loved ones at home" in some- thing in the way of cost between a few pence and a few shillings—so poor that it is to be hoped Santa Claus will come to their rescue on the eve of Christmas.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Several letters are held over in the unusually crowded state of our columns.
Lord Randolph Churchill has found and dc.‘- stroyed a cobra in South Africa; buf surely he did not need to go so far from home to find "snakes in the grass."

A six months' delay in a Chancery Suit as to some Buenos Ayres bonds has resulted in the bonds depreciating from £lO,OOO to £6,000; and out of the -26,000 the costs are to be paid. A Chancery suit suits lawyers but not litigants.

It is stated that the Queen will open Parlia- ment in person, in February. That sort of thing does happen now and again when the Tories are in office. Lord Salisbury has doubtless sought this mark of Etoyal favour; but it is the herald of his extinction as Prime Minister. After the opening, there will be the dissolution.

Sir Richard Brooks is announced as the Union- ist candidate for Rossendale in case of Lord Hart- ington being elevated to the House off Lords conse- quent upon the death of his father, the Duke of Devonshire. Sir Richard is a local man who received his title for his devotion to Lord Hart- ington. Be will be a strong candidate.

A Runcorn publican was convicted, on Monday, of permitting drunkenness. In the course of the hearing of the case, it was stated that Messrs. Greensll, Whitley and Co. made it a rule to turn out the tenant in case of a conviction. This is of course to protect their interests, but what of the interests of the publican who has to leave? And what about compensation ?

Another little war in the far north of India ; but nobody seems to know what it is all about. Perhaps it will transpire after an expenditure of men and money, that we have been meddling and muddling at Gilget as at Manipur. What about our occupation of Egypt? Is it not about time for John. Bull to ask himself if the game is worth the candle ? It has cost him in hard cash close on £15,000,000 already.

The Building Societies in Warrington are thriv- ing, and there is another in course of formation. There is plenty of room for all of them; kr the lesson of thrift has yet to be learned in many homes. In connection with two of the Starr- Bowkett Societies, there were appropriations on Monday. In each case the ballot resulted in .a title to £4OO free of interest for 121 years. This will come as a nice Christmas present to the for- tunate members.

Last night Mr. Robert Pierpoint, chairman of the Warrington Conservative Association, an- nounced his compliance with the request to be- come the candidate of the party at the next election. It would seem from the delay that he has been uncertain whether to say " yes " or "no." Health and cash have had to be considered; and it is just possible he may have heard that there are some Conservatives with whom he is anything but a favourite. However he is "in for it "now— sink or swim.

There has been bad management of " Peter's " and other" pence" at the Vatican. According to an official report of the commission of Cardinals the speculations of Monsignor Falchi, who had charge of the Vatican investments, have resulted in a loss of fully :20,000,000f. It is understood that not very long ago the amount of the losses stood at between 30,000,000 f, and 35,000,000 f." The money is gone, and Monsignor Falchi ought to " begone " too, if that is the best he can do.

The Austrian statue to He me does justice, ac- cording to the reports, to the genius of the satirist and poet. Heine is a favourite as an author of the Empress Elizabeth ; and he will become more of a favourite in this country as his works are better known. Mr. Walter Scott publishes a selec- tion of his poems in the Canterbury Poets series, price one shilling. Heine hits himself off when he says :
I laugh too, at the apes that look so wise, And swell themselves to arbiters of thought

The students of the Warrington School of Art have taken more than an average share of the South Kensington prizes; and Mr. Aylward, the headmaster, has every reason to be satisfied with the result of his and their labours. Competition gets keener every year; but, as the exhibition of work shows, local students are determined not to be left behind. In every department there is a distinct advance; and some of the students give ample evidence of versatile capacity. The Corporation are about to take over the school under most favourable auspices.

What with floods of water, slips of land, and lax management, the Ship Canal is very much in evidence. The shareholders need to have patience, and broad backs, for they have a great deal to bear. They are getting no interest for their capi- tal, and, as their interests are very much at stake, they are taking the right course in forming a Special Committee. No doubt all will come right "when the ship" lands, but it is a long way off landing at Manchester, and it will never land at all at Warrington if the Corporation do not show a firm front and battle for the rights of the town.

The Princess of Wales, like the good wife and good mother that sheis, has been anxiously nurs- ing her son Prince George; and now that he is improving she -is feeling the strain and is herself indisposed. How welr she wears in every way—in appearance, and in the affections of the people. Tennyson wrote like an inspired prophet in his "Welcome," in 1863, to the "Sea-Kings' daughter from over the sea." "Come to us, and love us, and make us your own " he exclaimed; and she has done so. Who does not hope that hr Royal Highness will soon be well enough to enter with spirit into the arrangements for the Royal Marriage?

Judging from his speeches this week in Scotland, Mr. Chamberlain is still dreaming of a new "National Party." The chief Tory organ the London "Standard "is getting somewhat impa- tient of this sort of nonsense, for it says :—" This has been the dream of a great many statesmen. But we do not seem to be much nearer to it now than we ever were. In the meantime Mr. Cham- berlain thinks the Liberal Unionists will be able to help the Conservatives more effectually as an independent party than by actually joining and becoming fused with them. This state of parties however, cannot last indefinitely, and the Liberal Unionists will eventually have to choose between 1 the Conservatives and the Gladstonians."

At Great Sankey Church, on Sunday morning, somebody's dog took a seat,but was not allowed to keep it, being turned out. Can it be that our canine worshipper thought it was Chrstmas Day? There is a quaint ancient rhyme which runs : Old woman get up and bake your pies, It's Christmas Day in the morning ; Bells are ringing. And cats are singing, And dogs are going to church; some with rags, And some with tags, And some with ruffle shirts.
How those old rhymes cling to the mind. "As I lay on the sunny bank" seems to be a favourite in Warrington at Christmastide ; for the sing-at-your-
CAMDEN WESLEYAN SINDAT SCHOOL, RIINCO RN.

The service of song entitled "The last look was ren- dered in this school, on Monday evening by the Camden orchestral band and choir. Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., presided, and the Rev. W. Arrowsmith read the narra- tive. The proceeds were added to the funds of the Band of Hope in connection with the school.

SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES. George Fairclough, clogger, Lacey.st.,was found dead in bed on Thursday morning. For six months past he had been subject to paralytic fits but had been able to follow his employment. About half-past one on Thurs- day morning he was seized with a fit, but he appeared to recover, and his mother left him. About six o'clock he was found dead. Dr. Allen who was called in said death had taken place about four hours previously,

FREE SCHOLARSHIPS AT FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL. At a competitive examinatipn lately held at the Grammar School, there were seventeen competi- tors, and free scholarships were awarded to W. A. Hague, of SO, Mersey-road, and J. W. Ashley, of 34, Oakland-st.• both of whom were pupils of Mr. • Snoddy, of the West Bank Board School. RUNCORN SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE. •

THE " PROFANITY " OF RUNCORN. Samuel Morris, described as a professional runner from Widnes, was brought up, under a warrant, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, charged with having used obscene and profane language. P.S. Gosling said about half-past two o'clock on Sunday morning, the 15th Nov- ember, the defendant and two other men catne across Runcorn Bridge, and passed out without giving up tickets or paying their fare. The ticket collector asked witness to aid him in collecting the fares, and he did so. The defendant made use of some filthy expressions, and said if witness wanted his name and address, he must catch him. Witness followed him to the railway station, and took him into custody just as he was getting into the Liverpool train. One of the defendant's companions had previously paid the fare.—By Mr. Knowles: The men said they had not booked because the man at the Widnes end was asleep.—Mr. Knowles, who defended, said during his fourteen years' experience he had only known one case of profane swearing, and he argued that this was an offence that ought to be corrected by the religious bodies, either Church or Dissent and not by the magistrates in a Police Court. If every person who made use of profane or obscene language were summoned to that Court there would be few even in that respectable neighbourhood who at one time or another would not occupy the unenviable position of defendant in that Court. He characterised the affair as a paltry and trivial matter.—Mr. Brundrit said evidently from Mr. Knowles's statement they were evidently purer in Widnes, for they had lots of cases of this sort.—The de- fendant was fined ss. and costs 17s.

div.p: TB E EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, DECEMBER 19, 1891

MILTON Li TERARY SOCIETY, WIDNES. The weekly meeting of this society was held on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. W. Harrison, B.A. A very instructive lecture was delivered by Mr. U. Warner on " Photography." The lecture was made interesting by lime-light illustrations. FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS AT WESTON POINT. At Weston Point on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest on the bady of William Whitley, a dock weighman who died on the 14th inst. from injuries received through falling downstairs at his home on the night of sth inst. and fracturing his skull. A verdict of accidental death was recorded.
THE WIDNES BASE COININE CASE.

On ThursTa;;,-;t—trie.- Liverpool Assizes. Frederick Lloyd, 'l'. Morris, and Ada Bedford were charged with passing base coin at Widnes, in August last. Lloyd, who had previoufly been convicted for similar offences, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude ; Morris was sentenced to three months' hard labour, and Ada Bedford to six months'. A THIEF AT RUNCORN.

Yesterday at Runcorn Police Court, Thomas Henry Russell, a native of Hamilton, Ontario, Canada, was committed to the Quarter Sessions on a charge of stealing three pairs of boots from the shop of Mr. T. Whinyates, Church-st., and slbs of ham and one tin of rabbit, the property of James Byrne, grocer, Church-st. The prisoner had been previously convicted.
position as nurse g?the Workhouse, and the resignation was accepted. The Clerk was instructed to advertise for a successor.

div.head: BURNING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: BURNING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

Yesterday Edwin Meek, mate of the Narrow boats Brand and Minnie belonging to Messrs. Simpson,Davies, and Co., met with a serious accident at Top Locks. Runcorn. The man is subject to fits, and, being sud- denly seized with one in the cabin of the Minnie he fell against the bars of the stove. His neck.face, and head were terribly burned,and onthe advice of Dr. McDougall he was removed to the Hospital. A few days ago the man fell into the canal in, a fit and had a narrow escape from death. GREENWAY ROAD EVENING SCHOOL SPELLING COMPETITION.

With a view to keeping up the interest of the pupils in their work, a " Spelling Bee " was arranged by the teachers of the above school, last Thursday evening. A large number of pupils competed, although entrance to the competition was optional. Much interest was taken in the proceedings,and two prizes, in the form of books, were given to the successful competitors. The winners' names are George McNorton,first prize,and Ernest Ward; second prize. It is the intention of the teachers to continue similar competitions during the ensuing session. PRESENTATION'S TO " Nox " HOUGHTON, OF RUNCORN. On Thursday evening a number of the personal friends and admirers of " Nox " Houghton, the full-back of the Runcorn Football Club, entertained him to tea at Riley's Café, Bridge-st., in honour of his selection for the North team. A good company sat down to the:excellent repast provided, and afterwards the evening was spent in a convivial manner. In the course of the proceedings,Mr. John Quirke, on behalf of the subscribers, presented Houghton with a handsome silver-mounted briar pipe, a pouch, and tobacco, and a gold breast pin, in recogni- tion of his past services, and as a mark of esteem. He received numerous congratulations on the honour con- ferred upon him.

BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIITY, SOCIETY. The twenty-ninth annual meeting of the Brunswick Mutual Improvement Society was held in the Brunswick School, on Wednesday evening. The proceedings com- menced with tea, to which about twenty members sat down. Ma subsequent meeting Mr. T. -Simister, presi- dent, occupied the chair. One of the secretaries, Miss Crosby, read the annual report,which showed the society to be in a flourishing condition. Mr. Simister was re- elected president, and Mr. J. D. Jones vice-president. Misses Simister and Crosby having held the office of secretaries for two years, asked to be relieved from the duties. A cordial vote of thanks was passed to them, and Mr. J. H. Darlington was appointed secretary for the coming year. The committee were re-elected, and the rest of the evening was spent with music and readings. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DurroN, Bankay-st., Warrington.—Advt. TOMMY BURNS'S RIVAL.

The St. Helens collier,John Dyer,who intended to dive from Walton Arches, Warrington, into the Mersey, on Saturday, postponed his feat, owing to the severe storm. Dyer on Saturday visited tho bridge, and feels confident of his ability to perform the dive. He has fully got over the effects of his dive from the Viaduct Bridge at Earlestown. PETROLEUM OIL.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Bridge-st., Warrington .—Advt. THE SALT UNION IN CHESHIRE.

The Mid-Cheshire salt trade continues in a most depressed condition, and a careful computation reveals the fact that over 250 workmen at North- wich and Winsford have been forced to find em- ployment at other places, chiefly at the Winnington and Lostock chemical works and Middlesborough. The shipments of white salt for the past month, 31,228 tons, have been several thousand tons less than the lowest shipments for November in any of the past ten years. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st. Warrington.—.Advt. THE WIDNES PERJURY CASE.

Yesterday week, at the Liverpool Assizes. before Mr. Justice Lawrance, William Clews, of Frederick- at., Widnes, surrendered to his bail to take his trial, on a charge of having wilfully committed perjury when giving evidence in a case in which the infor- mant was Elizabeth Ann Johnson, Prince's-st. lie was found guilty, and sentenced to six weeks' im- prisonment, his lordship remarking that very little was thought of committing perjury in these sort of cases, but in his sentence he had taken into con- sideration the prisoner's previous good character. RITCSEN R ANGERS.—Garland Builders Ironmonger, War rington.— Advt. DBOIDING TO MARRY TUB PROBRCIITRIX._

At—the Liverpool Assize-s, (Crown court), on Wed- nesday, before Mr. Justice Lawrence, a foreigner, named Joseph Schrember, aged 27, was charged with having indecently assaulted Catherine Marks, aged 15, the daughter of his landlady, on the sth November at Widnes. The prosecutrix stated that the prisoner was courting her, and had had the bans put up. The prisoner now informed the court that he still wished to marry the girl, and being asked did she consent the prosecutrix replied in the affir- mative. Without hearing the whole of the evidence for the prosecution, the judge dismissed the case. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-it., Warrington.—flevt.

div.head: AQUEDUCT TUNNEL UNDER THE MERSEY.
div.p: THE AQUEDUCT TUNNEL UNDER THE MERSEY.

G-. P. Deacon laid before the Water Committee of the Liverpol Corporation, on Tuesday, the sub- joined report as to the progress of the operations at Fiddler's. Ferry connected with the Vyrnwy aque- duct tunnel under the Mersey :—"The work already reported of removing the air-lock in the Lancashire shaft was completed on Tuesday last. During the remaining 3-1 working days of last week the air-lock in the tunnel was used, and a further distance of 314 ft. was driven, making the total distance finished &Mt. from the centre of the Lancashire shaft. The Corporation having taken up the work themselves, recommenced driving on the evening of the 12th tilt., and from that time to the evening Jf the 12th inst, the distance driven has been 119 feet 91 inches. UMBRELLAS RECovEnED.--T. and W. Durrox, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adv. _ _

THE LATE MR. CLARKE ASPINALL, At a special meeting of the Executive Cmiamittee of the Diocesan Church of England Temperance Society, held at the offices of the Society immedia- tely after the funeral, the Bev. Canon Penrhyn, rector of Winwick, presid.ng, the following resolu- tion was unanimously adopted by a largely attended meeting :—" That the members of the Liverpool ,Diocesan Church of England Temperance Society Executive Committee desire to place on record the deep sense of the irreparable loss which has been sustained through the death of their re- spected and beloved chairman, Mr. Clarke Aspinall. They also desire to convey to Mrs. Clarke Aspinall and family the expression of their sincere sympathy with•them in the sad bereavement which they have been called upon to bear." UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. & W. DurroN,Sankey-street. Warrington.—Advt.

PRESCOT BARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held on Thursday afternoon, Mr. J. Burchall presiding. There were also present the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. Tyrer, Middlehurst, Marsh, J. Goldsworth, Burrows, W. B Longton, Wareing, Hulme, E. Birchall, J. Birchall, Ran son, Ellison, Kenwright, Lowe, Griffiths, P. Longton- Daine, and A. F. Mann (clerk). RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 643 inmates this week, 596 last week and 584 in the corresponding period last year. Outdoor relief had been granted to 1,046 persons at a cost of £243 2s. 2d., against a similar number at a cost of £2OB 2s. 7d. last week. _ _

Wow' FOR TEE UNEMPLOYED.—On the recommenda- tion of the Visiting Committee the Guardians decided to again put into force an order adopted in 1834 for the employment of able-bodied men. The Clerk stated that in 1884 the order provided that relief would not be given to able-bodied single men. Married men would be relieved to the amount of is. 3d. per day with ?.d. per head for his children.. One half of the relief would be in kind. Men so relieved were required to be at the Workhouse from nine o'clock in the morning until tour o'clock in ths afternoon and would have dinner provided for them at the Workhouse. It was stated that the master of the Workhouse had received instructions to provide work for such applicants. RESIGNATION.—Miss 'Whitfield wrote resigning her

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

On Tuesday the usual monthly meeting of the abov• Board was held in the Widnes Town Hati,Mr. T.S.Timmis,J.P.,in the chair. There were also pre- sent—Dr. McDonnell, Major Wareing, Messrs. C. .13, Barlow, S. Quinn, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.-RESIGNATIONS.
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.-RESIGNATIONS.

The Committee recommended that the resignations of the Misses Irving, Clegg,Naylor, Ward, Clarke, and Mr. W. J. Davies be accepted from December, 1891. The Committee also recommended that the following teachers be appointed to the positions,and at the salaries specified, rising according to the scale of the Board :—Mr. E. B. Haddock, certificated assistant, senior boys' department of Simms Cross School, at a salary of £7O per annum ; Miss M. E. Naylor, head mistress of junior boys' depart- ment, at a salary of £B7. Miss J. E. Moody, certificated assistant of senior girls' department of Warrington-road School, at a salary of £65 per annum ; Miss M. R. Brown, ex-pupil teacher' of Senior girls department of. Warritigton-read schools, at a salary of £35 per annum; Miss M. J. Davies, ex-pupil teacher, of infants department at Warrington-road school, at a salary of £35 per annum ; Miss F. Clegg, head mistress of senior girls' department at West Bank School, at a salary of £llO per annum ; Miss J. Gardner, certificated assistant of the senior girls at West Bank, at a salary of £65 per annum ; Miss S. E. S. Wendt, ex-pupil teacher of junior boys at West Bank, at a salary of £35 per annum; Miss A. A. Robinson, ex- pupil teach f r of infants at West Bank, at a salary of £32. The Committee recommended that Miss Moore be appointed teacher of composition and writing at the central classes of pupil teachers (in the place of Miss Warp, resigned), at a salary according to the scale of the Board, the engagement to commence January Ist. 1892, and to be determinable on either side by one month's notice, to expire on the last day of any calendar month. The Committee further recommended that Harnaah Twigg be appointed as a monitor at a salary of £5 per annum, the engagement to date from January Ist, 1892. Her salary, if engaged as a pupil teacher, to commence from September first, 1892, if she passes the Government examination. It was rec-o-fifinended that the salaries of the following teachers be increased as under, in accor- dance with the rules of the Board ; the increase to date frons January Ist, 1892 : •

It was recommended that on and after January Ist, 1892, no school fees should be charged in any of the in- fant schools under the Board. It was decided to adopt the recommendation of the Committee with regard to the abolition of the fees in the infant schools, and to leave the other matter for discussion at a special meet- ing.

div.head: SITES AND BUILDING COMMITTEE.
div.p: SITES AND BUILDING COMMITTEE.

The Committee recommended that the following tenders be accepted for the repairs required at the vari- ous Board Schools :—Mr. J. Beech (Simms' Cross), Mr. C. J. Sutcliffe (Warrington-road), and Messrs. D. Lea and Sons (West Bank.)

div.head: ABSENCE OF MR. R. H. DAVIS.
div.p: THE ABSENCE OF MR. R. H. DAVIS.

The Chairman stated that in accordance with an Act of Parliament in 1870, if a member was absent for six consecutive meetings of the Board his seat became vacant. Mr. Davis was placed in that circumstance, and he was sure they all sympathized with him, and re- gretted the cause which prevented him from being pre- sent; but the Act stipnlated certain causes which exempted him from resigning. He therefore proposed that Mr. Davis still be a member of the Board, and that the Clerk be instructed to send him a message of sym- pathy from the Board.—Major Wareing seconded the proposition, and said he fully recognized Mr. Davis's valuable services on the Board. The proposition was unanimously carried.
IMPORTANT ACTION RE WATER RATES AT WIDNES. • •

Before His Honour Judge Shand at Widnes County Court, yesterday, the Widnes Local Board sued seven builders for payment of their water rates. The defendants were Charles Hemingway, J. W. Carlile, Richard Balshaw, Sayce and Randle, C. J. Sutcliffe and J. Loins.—Mr. Squarey, barrister (instructed by Mr. H. S. Oppenheim) appeared for the Local Board, and Mr. J. Pickford, barrister (in- structed by Mr. C. H. Lewin) appeared for the defend- ants.—The seven eases were taken together. The prot coedings were taken under the Widnes Improvement Ac- of 1867, and the cause of the dispute was a minimum charge of ss. made for water consumed by meter. Previ- ous to June 1890, the charge for water for other than domestic purposes was 51. per 1,000 gallons, but at that time the Local Board reduced the price to qd. and at the same time passed a resolution that the minimum charge for water should be ss. Several of the defendants had signed an agreement to pay this minimum charge, while others had not done so but had received notice of the charge, but the agreement signed by Mr. Beech and Messrs. Sayce and Randle did not continue the clause with re- gard to the charge. Mr. Squarey argued that the Local Board had the power by their Ka to vary the charges for water at their discretion, and that this was a reasonable charge and one made by other public bodies. Mr. Pickford, on the other hand, contended that it was altogether unreasonable, and referred to the case of Mr. Hemingway, who besides paying for the fixing of a meter and a water rent was called upon to pay for two quarters a minimum charge of ss. although not a drop of water had passed throtigh the meter. His Honour said water was supplied at qd. and did not that enter into the consideration of the Board in fixing the minimum charge, and if it did was it unreasonable? Mr. Pickford in reply pointed out that the difference between the old rate of 51. per 1,000 gallons, and the present price made a difference of 30s. to Mr. Hemingway and the others also lost in preportion. This charge was a matter of indifference to the consumers, and it worked hardly against the small consumers who could least afford it. —His Honour said the point to be decided was whether the Board had a right to make an alteration in the water rate, and whether it was a fair and reasonable thing to make that stipulation about the minimnm oharge.—Mr. Square quoted a section of the Act to show that the Board had this power.—His Honour reserved judgment, after hearing a number of witnesses.
DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. TOWNS,
OF RUNCO RN.

We record with regret the death of Mr. W. Towns of Leinster Gardens, Runcorn, which took place at his residence on Saturday last after a long and painful illness. A native of South Shields, Mr. Towns was early in life identified with the chemi- cal trade, and 16 years ago he came to Runcorn to undertake the management of the works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele. He occupied that position until about 18 months ago. when he transferred his services to Widnes, where lie took control of the large works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co. In beth positions Mr. Towns, while fully protecting and forwarding the in- terests of his employers, gained the respect and esteem of the workmen, and amongst the townspeople generally his character was held in high estimation. He was an active Churchman and occupied the position of people's warden at the Parish Church. He also took a great in- terest in the doings of the Football Club, of which he was a vice-president. The deceased gentleman had only attained the are of 46 years. The funeral took place on Thursday afternoon in the presence of a large concourse of people. Besides the mourners and towns- people about 150 workmen from Messrs. Hutchinson's and Messrs. W'igg's works took part in the procession. The cortege first proceeded to the Parish Church, where a full choral service was gone through by the choir and the Rev. J. Holden ; the organist (Mr. Johnson) play- ing the Dead March in " Saul " at the conclusion. The procession then wended its way to the cemetery where the burial service was read at the grave side by the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, M.A., vicar, and the choir sang" Brief Life is here our portion." The mourners included, besides the sons and relatives of the deceased, the following gentlemen : Dr. McDougall, Dr. Carruthers,Messrs. Michael Barker' J. E. Meredith, W. Rogerson, T. Kirkham, G. Moss, W. Timmins, E. Alarwood, J. Littler, J. Speakman. J. Morrison (district manager of the United Alkali Com- pany). S. Pope (manager Messrs. Hazlehurst's works), F. J. Norman (manager Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele's works), and the following representing Messrs. Hutchin- son's works :—Messrs. J. H: Taylor. W. Treacy, G. H. Hedley, A. Caton, J. C. Smith, W. E. Oakden, A. G. Kyle, A. G. Wright, J. Smith, C. Evans, J. S. Hunt, A. W. Dwerryhouse, F. Cave, J. Donoghue. T. Barton, J. McConoghy, M. Cain. J. W. Bottomley, J. Barney, and C. Abrams. The following employs ot Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele showed a last tribute of respect to their

late manager by joining in the procession :—Messrs. C. A. Dawson, J. Turnbull, J. H. Turnbull,' J. Turnbull, jun., J. Bostock, P. Thomas, T. Withington, J. Slaingler, A. Clucas, J. Williams, R. Wainwright, W. Wainwright T. Lucas,J. Ellis, J. Woodcock G. Bradshaw, J. Whitley, W. Johnston, D. Pilgrim, J. Durr,S. Ashley, R. Woodward M.. Carr. J. Hofliand, S. Cox, J. Ashley, T. Crow, A. ,Lewis, J. Jolley, T. Johns,m, J. Shaw, J. Chesters, R. Hall, R. Reece, J. Gatley, J. Ford, W. Faulkner, J. France, T. Davies, W. Hardcastle, J. Owen, J. Ashley, sent, E. Ashley, T. Pierce, J. Brazendale, J. Gaskell, W. W.l.6dcock.W. Hedgecock, J. Jollev,W. Cutlip, P. Loath- d, S. Hignett, J. Newall, J. Wilson, J. Ellison, and 'F.• Clarke. The Runcorn Football Club, in which de- ceasfed took great interest, was represented by Messrs. H. Hughes, J. E. Langshaw, and J. H. Crompton. Among the many wreaths sent were the following : From AN.. and Mrs. J. Hadley (Liverpool), Messrs. Albert Penningt4n, Edgar S. Lea, Clement Handley, and T. Dunbavand, members of the Parish Church Council, Mr. and Mrs. Johnson,Mr. and Mrs. J. Littler,Miss Statham, Mr. and Mrs. Ellison, Mr. and Mrs. F. J. Norman, em- ployes of Messrs. Hutchinson (Widnes), Mr. C. H. R. Harrison, employes Hull and Liverpool Red Oxide, Corn- pany, members of the Runcorn Football Club,foremen of Hutchinson's work office staff, Mr. and Mrs. Wilson,Mr. and Mrs. J. J. Speakman,and Old Quay Copper Works. The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. Hewitt, and the mourning coaches and hearse were sup- , plied by Messrs. Yarwood Bros. During the evening muffled peals were rung on the bells of the Parish Church.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
"By AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

The judgment of the Technical Education Com- mittee in selecting the Town Hall site for the proposed Institute, has been endorsed by Mr. Bow- don, C.E. of Manchester. This gentleman paid a visit to the town,on Wednesday,and made a careful examination of the plot of land, and he unhesitat- ingly stated that it was admirably adapted for a technical school, and he gave the sub-committee, who lisve the matter in hand, some valuable advice, It is a matter for congratulation that the site has proved so satisfactory, as the ratepayers will be saved the expense of purchasing land in another part of the town at a cost of several hundred pounds, and this important initial step having been con- cluded, the committee will now doubtless at once procure plans and push on the construction of the building with all speed, so that ere another winter arrives the school may be in thorough working ' order, if this be possible.

Runcorn Musical Society give their second con- cert of the season on Monday evening next, and the high standard of excellence which has been charac- teristic of the society since its inception will, if the programme be a guide, be maintained. The voca- lists engaged are in the first rank, the band and chorus have always been up to their work in the past, and we ought to have such a rendering of Rossini's sacred cantata " Stabat Mater' as will amply repay the: expenditure ot time and money. The second part of the programme con4ists of mis- cellaneous items.

The schoonsr Blanche, of Runcorn, left Falmouth for this port on Sunday, the 6th inst., and, as no- thing has since been heard of her, it is feared that she has foundered and all bands lost. The master was Captain John Owen, of Dukes Field,and his son acted as mate. Much sympathy is expressed for the three motherless daughters in their suspense. The schooner belonged to Mr. Reade. a relative of Mr.S. B. Chadwick, J.P. A large -number of vessels that have arrived in the port during the last ten days have been more or less damaged.

The chemical workers of Widnes and Runcorn are not looking forward to Christmas with those feel- ings of pleasureablti anticipation which are usually at*ociated with this festive season of the year. Notices have been posted up in all the yards that work will be suspended for nine. days from Thurs- day December 24th, and this means not only a great loss to the whole of the men,but to many who have not provided for a rainy day great privation at a time when the tables are wont. to be covered with more plenteous provision than on any other occasion. The reason I have heard for this long stoppage is that the stocks have become very large, and that it will be a favourable opportunity for carrying out repairs and taking stock. Perhaps, however things may not be so bad as they appear. The managers of the various works may" sub" the men until they again resuige work. If there be not something done, there is ik doubt that huge de- mands will be made upon the poor rate in Widnes, to keep the people from starving,

div.head: GROVE HOUSE SCHOOL, RUNCORN.
div.p: GROVE HOUSE SCHOOL, RUNCORN.

The conclusion of the Christmas term of this school, of which Mrs. Soulby is the principal, was signalised by the holding of an exhibition of pic- tures in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Wednesday afternoon, and a pianoforte recital in the evening. The collection of drawings in chalk and paintings in oil and water colours, was a very fine one, and they had been hung and draped with much taste, and to the best advantage considering the wall space avail- able. They were all the 'work of the class pupils and private pupils of Miss J. Pierpoint, the art mistress to the school, and were highly creditable to the artistes and to their teacher. That several of the pupils posses- sed exceptional talent was plainly evident, and the standard of merit all through was very high. The ex- hibition was attended by a numerous company of ladies and gentlemen. A display of charming old china kindly lent for the occasion by Mrs. Deakin of Simms Cross, Widnes, attracted much attention and was greatly admired.

IR the evening the pupils of Miss Kate Clegg., the teacher of music, gave a pianoforte recital,which was re- garded as a rich musical treat by the large audience that had assembled. A Steinway grand piano, given by Mr. Temperley's establishment, in Lowland-road, was used, and the programme was as follows :—Overture "William Tell," the Misses 13. Wallington and F. Firbank ; sonatina in G, Miss Rose Tiley ; sonata in C. Op. 20, Miss Kirsty Forrester ; trio "The imps revels," the Misses K. Harri- son, F. Wilton, and D. Wallington; duet (violin and pianoforte), " Romance,- the Misses Nina and Kitty Harrison ; duet in D. Op. 6, the Misses Firbank and R. Tiley ; Sonatina in C. Op. 88,Miss E. Robinson ;Rondo Tillagois, Miss F. Firbank ; Balmoral, Miss M. Pope; duet, " The Lake," the Misses F. Timmins, and N. Harrison ; Minuet, Miss Hadfield ; Nocturne in D. flat Op. 24 : Impromptu in B. fiat Op. 142 ,Miss L. Peacock; duet, "Poet and Peasant," Misses C. Hadfield and M. Pope; Andante in F. major, Miss Soulby ; Sonato C sharp minor "Moonlight," Miss C. Hadfield; overture" Caliph of Bagdad," the Misses Soulby and Hadfield ; Sonata " Maid of Orleans," Miss Wallington.
WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.

The annnal distribution of prizes in connection with th, classes took place in the Baths Assenibly room ott Thursday evening, and there was a fair company present. In the absence of Dr. O'Keeffe, Mr. H. Wade Deacon presided, and on the platform. were Dr. Campbell Brown (professor of chemistry, Liverpool University), Mrs. Campbell Brown, Dr.. Hurter, Mr. Driffield, Rev. R. G. Hughes, Rev. G. II Garrett, Mr. H. S. Oppenheim. The Chairman in open- ing the proceedings, said it was an excellent thing that the Local Board had undertaken to look after the Tech- nical instruction of the town in future, and it was a step that had the approval of all who had been connected with the Science and Art Classes. They all hoped that there would be more progress under the new arrange- ment than there was under the old, although good work had been done in the past. (Applause.) Mr. S. C. Hoyle, secretary to the Technical Instruc- tion Committee, read the following report :—ln pre- senting the report of the results of the examinations held in May last, I should mention the fact that it is the first report issued by the Widnes Local Board since they adopted the Technical Instruction Act, 1889,, and took over the Science and Art schools which were presented to them by the Widnes Science and Art Committee. Before proceeding with the reading of the report, I wish to refer to the great loss the Technical Instruction Com- mittee sustained by the death of the late secretary, Mr. .T. T. Allen, which happened shortly before the corn- mencetnent of the examinations. The Committee have recorded upon their minutes, their appreciation of the services he rendered, and of the zeal and ability with which he laboured in the interests of the people of Widnes. The students under instruction in 1890,91 numbered 131, the entries to the various classes numbering 184. The number of students who presented themselves for ex- amination, and the number of certificates obtained, were as follows :

No.exarnined Passed Per cent Art........................... 26 ... 5 ... 19 Plane and solid geometry ...... 12 ... 9 ... 75 Machine construction Building construction 6 ... 4 ... 57 Inorganic chemistry (theoretics.l) 38 ... 16 ... 42 Inorganic chemistry (practical) 19 ... 14 ... 74 Aulmal physiology

120 65 The percentage of passes in plane ancl solid geometry% machine constructi,m, practical chemistry and animal physiology were exceplionally goad ; on comparing the average percentage of pasFes in all the subjects, I find tbe.t the averav of the Widnes stwle.nts it-5. 2 per

cent. better than the a erage obtained by the total num- ber of students who presented themselves at the examin- ations held in connection wit!'h the department of Science and Art. The Technical Instraction Committee fully re-, cognise the importance of providing. an effective and complete system of Technical Education, and they have appointed a sub-committee to consider the question of erecting Technical Schools, and to formulate a complete scheme of lechnical Education for this District. This question is now receiving the careful consideration of the Committee, and they have recently visited the Stockport Technical School ,which is considered one of the most complete Technical Schools in the kingdom. The Committee hope that ere long a building will be erected which will be not only a credit to the town, but also pro- vide ample accommodation for the rapidly increasing number of students who are availing themselves of the facilities for obtaining technical instruction. (Applause.) Mrs. Campbell Brown then distributed the prizes awarded to the successful students, a list of which has previously been published in this journal. Mr. Campbell Brown, in the course of an address, expressed his pleasure at being present on that occasion and,alluding to the adoption of the Technical Instruction Act, said the teaching of science and art could not and ought not to continue to be dependent upon private and individual benevolence. The whole nation was depen- dent on the knowledge of its workers, and on that knowledge being ample, and the necessity of teaching everyone engaged in manufactures, or any kind of con- structive activity had become more impressed upon the public mind of late years, and the public and the legislature had recognised the necessity of mak- ing great and consistent effort to promote what was denominational Technical Education if we were to out- strip our rivals in other parts of the world. Ezeryone to some extent benefited directly or indirectly by the spreading of sound knowledge, and now every house- holder in Widnes contributed as he ought some small fractional sum towards providing this education. He pointed out where the present school required improve- ment, and suggested the teaching of several branches of knowledge not now in the curriculum. Alluding to German competition in manufactures, Dr. Brown said the Germans were progressing mote rapidly than the English, and unless we were. to be seriously beaten by them, we must progress equally or more. One reason for the progress of the German manufacturer was that they did not despise small industries. Now the English- man preferred large industries—could not be bothered with them. Now, the German would take an immense amount of trouble to make things which were only required in small quantities and would take as much trouble to get orders for them as the Englishman would take for large orders of goods made upon a large scale. Then the German paid his unskilled labourers less than we did, but at the same time he paid his chem- ists and skilled workers more than did the average Eng- lish manufacturer. The forecast was that the English to keep their manufacturing industries and their trade would have to pay their unskilled workers less and their skilled workers more. Therefore he who wanted to get on should endeavour to get as far as he could from the ranks of the unskilled workers and as high as he could in the ranks of the skilled workers, and these science and art classes were the means offered for helping them to rise in the scale. (Applause.) Mr. Brown concluded with the same advice to the students.—Mr. G. I. Neil moved a vote of thanks to Mrs. Brown for distributing the prizes and Dr. Brown for his able address.—Dr. Hurter seconded,and said he did not think our labourers would like to hoar that their wages must be reduced. (Laughter.) She thought there would be another way of meeting that thing. suppose the English Chemi- cal labourers sent Dr. King over to Germany and made the German labourers ask for as much money as the English labourers, they should be all equal once more (Loud laughter.)—The motion was carried by acclama- tion and Dr. Brown in reply said he only told them what he believed to be the signs of the times.—Mrs. Brown also responded in a bright and humourous speech.—The Rev. G. H. Garrett proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, and through him to the other noble manufac- turers who had done so much for Technical Education in the past.—The Rev. R. G. Hughes seconded, and it was carried, and, the Chairman having replied, the meeting terminated.

THE CHARGE AGAINST A SCRIPTURE READER. On Saturday, at Colne, James Albert Mason, (36j, described as a refreshment house keeper and scrip- ture reader, was again placed in the dock, charged on remand, with bigamy. There was a large atten- danee.—William Heys, booking clerk at Edge Hill Station, Liverpool, spoke to being present at the prisoner's first marriage, at St. Catherine's Church, Wigan, on May 19th, 1890, and also at his trial for bigamy at Newton-le-Willows.—Mary Bannister, the prisoner's third wife, deposed that when she married him he said his name was Herbert James and that he was a single man. Prisoner, who had nothing to say, was committed for trial to the Man- chester Assizes.

STREET FOOTBALLING. At the borough police court, on Monday morning, Thomas and Peter Oakes, John Thos. Gleeson, Win. Fudge, Thos. Ellison, Dennis Dagnall, John Cavanagh, and Wm. Brodrick, boys, were charged with playing at football in Platt-street on the morning of the 10th inst. The constable who proved the charge said the ball was a soft one, and would not have hurt anybody. The Bench, however, fined the defendants is. each. THEFT OF A TUMBLER. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Wednes- day, Thomas George Leach, 37,Frederick-St., Latchford, was charged with stealing on the previous day, a tumb- ler glass, value 3d., the property of Joseph Ashton, of the Bridge Inn.—P.C. Amson deposed to seeing prisoner come out of the inn putting something in his pocket which appeared to be a glass. On the bridge he stopped him and asked him what he had got in his pocket. The prisoner replied " I don't know," but witness said he believed it was a glass, and then the prisoner pulled it out. Witness took him to the inn, and it was there found that a glass had been missed. Other evidence having been given,the prisoner was fined ss. ; in default seven days.

STEALING HAM. At the Warrington borough police court, on Monday, Joseph Johnson, labourer, from Northwich, was charged on remand with stealing, on the previous Friday after- noon, from the shop of Charles Price, Sankey-street, slbs. of ham, value 3s. 4d. The chief constable had received a communication from the police authorities at North- wich stating that a pair of boots, stolen from a shop, and a quantity of clothes, supposed to have been stolen, had been found at his lodgings. The prisoner, on being charged with the theft of the ham, replied " It is non- sense of me doing such a thing, for I was not in want. It is through my having a drop of drink." The chief constable remarked that there were rather too many of this sort of fellows coming into the town. Sometimes they were caught, and sometimes not.—The prisoner was sent to jail for a month's hard labour. CHARGE OP STEALING A SPADE AND A-SSAIITLT. At the Borough Police Court, -rnursday morning, Thomas Linney, and George Kent, navvies, were charged with stealing at the Leigh Arms, the previous day, a spade, from the person of Frederick Daw, a navvy, working at Twenty Step Bridge, Cheshire. The prisoners were also charged with assaulting Daw, on the same date.—For the prosecution it was stated that all three men were in the Leigh Arms, and Kent snatched the spade from Daw, went out and sold it for is. to Mrs. Leslie, general dealer, in Mersey-st.—Daw shouted to Kent to bring the spade back as he was going out with it, but he took no notice. He came back in about half- an-hour and offered Daw the shilling for which he had sold the spade, but Daw would not accept it.—Daw went out, and found where the spade had been sold, and came back with Mrs. Leslie, who pointed out Kent as the man who had sold her the spade.—Kent knocked him down, and Lilley also struck him and they used threatening lan- guage to him.—The evidence in support of the charges was given by the prosecutor, and W. Marrs, Mrs. Leslie, and D.S. Monaghan.—The prisoners said they had sold their shovels for is. each to get drink, and Daw asked Kent to sell his for him.—Daw denied this, but admitted that he had meant selling his.—The prisoners were dis- missed on the charge of theft, but fined ss. and costs on the second charge.

ASSAULT o A LANDLORD.—WiIIiam 'Robinson was charged with ben.' drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting Joseph Nichols on his licensed premises in Victoria Vaults.—The complainant stated that defendant came into the tap room about 5.30 on Friday afternoon with two other men and created a disturbance. He was put out, and when he (witness) went to close the door, the defendant deliberately struck him on the head with a buckle end of a strap, inflicting a, lather serious wound. Be had previously been ill in bed;'hnd that was the irst time he had been up.—The defendant stated that he did not remember striking the complainant with a strap. He characterised the whole affair as a free fight. and said that everything he did was in self-defence..—The Bench coiimitted him to gaol for 21 days with hard labour. , MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman E. RUGBY. WIDNES v. WALDEN.—The first fixture between these two clubs this season was decided on Saturday, at Walkden, in favour of the latter by one goal and two tries (nine points) to nil. MATCHES ABANDONED AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN.—SHOW and rain fell at Runcorn and Widnes on Saturday morn- ing with the result that the fooLhall grounds were totally unfit to play upon. Widnes "A " should have played Earleztown, but a wire was despatched to the latter, saying the ground was unfit. Clifton should have visited Widnes to play St. Mary's, but this fixture was also abandoned. The fixtures between Runcorn and Swinton "A " teams and Garsten Copperworks and Earlestown Albion were not played, owing to the bad weather.

SWINTON V. RUNCORN At Swinton, in miserable weather, before 1,500 specta- tors, Runcorn kickel off, and soon forced the home team to defend their lines. Marsh, however, got away, but was brought back for" off-side." Swinton took play to the visitors' "25," and Pearson get over, but the ball was ordered back. Swinton were awarded a pen- alty kick in a good position, bus Paul just sent the leather wide. Horton for the visitors, got in a brilliant kick, and play was transferred to midfield. The Swin- ton forwards came away with a grand rush,and Brockle- bank, getting possession, transferred to Marsh, the lat- ter of whom riggled through the ruck of his opponents I • and gained a beautiful try in a favourable position,from which Valentine landed a fine goal. The Runcorn backs got away, but Paul with a splendid kick relieved nicely, and again the visitors had to defend. Nothing further transpired up to half-time, when Swinton was leading by a goal to nothing. Resuming, Talentine got off with a good run, and passed to Pearson, but the latter was brought down finely. A smart bit of passing among the -visitors' three-quarters and a good punt by Pendlebury took play to the home territory, when S. Abrahams wa..s conspicuous with some neat work. Marsh was again prominent with a brilliant run and kick, but nothing came of it. The visitors got away with a good rush,but Valentine was an obstacle, and prevented danger. Swin- ton was hotly pressed towards the finish, but Marsh was again to the front and transferred play to mid-field. Dolan had to retire, Horton was hurt in the last few minutes and the final result was :—Swinton 1 goal, (5 points) ; Runcorn nothing. WARRINGTON V. LEEDS PARISH CHURCH. The severe weather which prevailed throughout the country on Saturday affected this match at Leeds. The Warringtonians had made anlearly:journey, and arrived at the Yorkshire town soon after one• ,o'clock, but on their arrival a heavy snowstorm'set in, and the outlook of a match being played_looked bad. However, the Leeds Executive had taken a "gate," and Warrington had no alternative but to face the elements. The storm had increased, it anything, and coupling this with the' intense cold, matters were anything but agreeable. Warrington having won the toss, attacked the town goal, before a meagre attendance, only about 700 being present. Oddy kicked off, and Boscow and Waddington having replied in turn, Turner showed up in leading the visiting forwards well into the Leeds' 25, Ryan saving well. A penalty kick to the homesters enabled Oddy to find touch at half-way, but a brilliant display between the two Bates and Evans saw the latter putting in a grand run, being pulled up a yard from the line. Ryan and Mossley relieved, and Evans next tried a shot at goal, and a minor was scored. Webster and Heesom, with judicious kicks, raised an attack on the home goal, but Leeds, with a combined rush, forced the game on the Warrington line. The visitors defended as well as could be expected under the circumstances, and a rush, headed by Knowles and Holmes, and some exchanges between Eastwood, Waddington, and Boscow, found the oval once more at the Churchmen's quarters. Heesom made his mark cleverly, and Collin being at fault in the reply, the oval was taken over by Teare, but Eastwood kicked dead when the Warringtonian was in the act of grounding. The game now resembled more of a farce, the players apparently having had enough of it. No further points were scored during this half, and when the interval arrived an application was made to have the match abandoned. Leeds, however, would not lis- ten to the appeal, and the game was resumed. The snow had rendered the ground in a miserable state, and coupling this with the increased fall of snow, the players were scarcely distinguishable. So intense was the cold. that the men rarely fielded the ball, and relied on flying kicks to avert disaster. From what could be gathered from the general play, Leeds had a trifle the best of it, and succeeded in registering a couple of miners, both points being the result of drops at goal. Time brought a welcome relief to the players and an end to a miserable exhibition, the score reading as two minors each. eaois arrmgwii : J. Du., U. F. Heesom, and J. W. Evans, three-quarter backs; Jas. T. Bate, and John Bate, half backs; H. Ashton (capt.), Fair Turner, J. Knowles, A. Molyneaux, W. Randles, J. Holmes, T. Donohue, H. Teare, and J. Berry, forwards. Leeds Parish Church: T. Collin, back; J. Northend, S. Waddington, and S. Eastwood, three-quarter backs; Cl. Mossley and T. Ryan, half backs; T. Armitage, B. Dick- inson, J. Dickinson, G. English. J. Oddy, C. Richardson, H. Roberts, T. Stephens, and H. Walker, forwards.

The complainant said he came in drunk, and said he had done some work and had only got a paltry shilling, and had drunk it for vexation. He then said he would not have that young thing (meaning his stepson) sitting on the hearth, and doing nothing, but go to church, and thenhe attacked her, making her arm black and blue.— The defendant's stepson said the defendant wanted to sell up the furniture and this caused the quarrel.—The defendant said his wife stripped the house while he was out, and left him nothing to eat. He was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and pay the costs.

div.head: BRIGHTON MURDER.
div.p: THE BRIGHTON MURDER.

There is still great excitement in Brighton concerning the horrible murder of the child Edith Jeal. George Henry Wood, a railway porter, was again remanded at Brighton, on Tuesday, charged with wilfully murdering the little girl Edith Jeal. It was stated that the Public Prosecutor would take up the case, and also that the stains upon the prisoner's clothes would be carefully examined by an expert, and had been sent to Dr. Stev- enson for that purpose.

div.head: TERRIBLE DOUBLE MURDER.
div.p: TERRIBLE DOUBLE MURDER.

A cold-blooded double murder has been perpetrated in West Hertfordshire, at a village called Addbury. On Saturday night a gamekeeper named Puddephatt, and a watchman named Crawley, each aged 38, employed by Mi. J. Williams, of Pendley Tring, went to watch the Stocks Wood, and on Sunday morning the head game- keeper, found their dead bodies in a field near the woods. ThGir heads were terribly battered, apparently with gunstocks. It is believed they were deliberately mur- dered by poachers. The inquest on the deceased was opened on Monday evening, and adjourned after formal evidence had been takeu. On the same afternoon a man named Smith was arrested on suspicion of being con- cerned in the crime.

div.head: WATERFORD ELECTION.
div.p: WATERFORD ELECTION.

Waterford was the scene of serious rioting on Sunday. It had been announced that Messrs. Wm. O'Brien and M. Davitt would arrive in town, and ominous rumours were afloat as to what would happen. Messrs. Davitt, O'Brien, Condon, and Tanner were attacked by a crowd cf Waterford Parnellites. Stones were thrown and blackthorns vigorously wielded. In the rioting one young man struck Mr. Davitt a heavy blow upon his forehead, from which blood flowed freely,and Dr. Tanner was struck by a stone. Mr. J. Redmond, writes to a Liverpool correspondent denying that his acceptance of the candidature for Waterford was conditional on the local Parnellites pay- ing him £3OO per annum. Mr. Michael Davitt's address to the Waterford electors states that he pledges himself with the Irish Parliamen- tary party to obtain for Ireland such a measure of Home Rule as will satisfy the national aspirations of the people.
