div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

FOOTBALL.—ASSOCIATION. The draws for the Football Association and the Lanca- shire Cups took place during the past week. The ties will not be played off for some time, but they are ex- citing a good deal of interest. The present holders of the English Cup should come through the first round safely, as should the North End. But others of the League clubs will be less fortunate. Notts, for instance, can hardly hope for victory at Sunderland, and Burnley will do extremely well to win at Everton. Bolton Wan- derers are set a very hard task to knock out Sheffield Wednesday on the ground of the latter. The two clubs, it will be remembered, suet in the semi-final two years ago, when the Sheffielders just won, but were afterwards badly beaten by the Rovers in the final. Accrington will have to make the profitless journey to London to (ppose the Crusaders. Sheffield united can scarcely hope to beat Blackpool, whose form is suprisingly con- sistent.

There were some regrettable incidents at two of the League matches on Saturday. Perhaps the trying w4ather had its effects on some of the players, but whatever the cause there were at least two ugly outbreaks. At Deep- dale Oswald, the Notts centre forward, struck Drum- mond, and blows were exchanged. Both left the field, and there was further fighting near the dressing-room, Oswald, it seems, was ordered off, and the Prestonian followed him. In the second half all the Notts men ex- cept five retired, play being thus reduced to a farce. Noah End won by six goals to none. There was a similar scene at Turf Moor. Lofthouse made his re- appearance in the Rovers' team after a protracted absence, and there were repeated skirmishes between him and Stewart, a Burnley half back. This culmin- ated in the referee, Mr. Clegg, sending the pair off the ground, all the Rovers' players except Arthur also retir- ing. They declared the cold was more than they could stand. Burnley 'were then leading by three to nothing, but it is pretty certain that the game will have to be replayed. Mr. Clegg expressed his determination to bring tho offenders befort the Associ.tion.

There was only seven minutes' play at Accrington, where the full force of the storm was felt. Aston Villa were the visitors, and they will of course have to make anotlaer journey to the Lancashire town. Everton had only a goal to spare at the conclusion of their return with Wolverhampton Wanderers. Here, too, football was carried on amid very disagreeable surroundings. The Bolton Wanderers, are to be congratulated on their good fortune at Stoke, by which they are still at the head of the League. Sunderland toyed with Darwen, scoring as many as seven goals against them besides two that were disallowed. The Wearsiders can new boast of more goals in their favour than any of their rivals. West Bromwhich Albion were again in a winning vein, polish- ing off Derby County.

I somewhat significant fact in connection with the record of the Preston North End since they were recog- nised as a leading club is that whilst they have defeated all the leading organisations in England and Scotland by five goals or :more, not a single club has ever beaten North End by that number. This is something to be proud about, and the more you look at it the more creditable it appears. Another item in North End's career is that they have won every cup for wbich they have competed, viz., English, Lancashire, and League; and no other League club can say that, although the Rovers can, perhaps, point to a better performance by carrying off the English Cup five times, and they say this season will make up the half-dozen.

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

There is the usual expression of dissatisfaction with the team selected to do duty for the North against the South. It pleases nobody. Yorkshire are crying out because that undeniably smart forward Toothill has been passed over. As a hard worker he has no superior. Lancashire have been treated with a very niggardly hand. To select only three of their representatives is not doing them justice. Pyke, the St. Helens forward, de- served a place if anybody did. The te..tm has been made up from so many different shires that the combi- nation is sure to suffer,and this will tell in favour of the Southerners. Alderson has been given the preference over Marsh despite his erratic form against Cheshire and the fine play of the Swintonian all through the season. Taylor can hardly be compared with Berry as a half back, but the latter is not so safe as he ought to be, and that is the reason he has been shelved.

The sudden visitation of wintry weather quite spoiled football on Saturday. In many cases teams did not strip, whilst in others two " twenties" were just about as much as the players could endure. Some of the grounds were in a terrible condition, several being actually under Water.

Marsh was largely responsible for the success of Swin- D-,monr.- The try which he secured was a splendid piece of work, as he made his way host of antagonists, and Valentine xicked a goal from the easy place. Swinton are sure to miss Marsh when he leaves for Scotland. He never played so well as he has done this season, and if his merits met with their just reward he would attain the highest honours. After his departure Valentine will very probably take up the position of centre thred-quarter, with Winterbottom and Pearson on the wings.

The Rugby Union Board are to be asked to settle a question which will be watched with some curiosity. A firm of pianoforte dealers have offered one of their in- struments for the club that wins the Yorkshire Cup,and a certain newspaper intends presenting £45 to the most successful Rugby team of the season. Can these gifts be accegted without violating the laws of amateurism? It is a nice point, and the ruling of the Union will be very important.
We understand that the match between Warrington and Runcorn teams has been postponed till later in the season, probably in February when the days are longer.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN AMERICA. THIRTY PEOPLE KILLED. NEW YORE, THURSDAY.—A serious railway accident occurred on the Pittsburg, Fort Wayne, and Chicago Railway at Lima, Ohio, yesterday. A train, known as the Columbian express, ran off the line and was wrecked thirty persons being killed and thirty others injured,four injured.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S DIVORCE CASE
div.p: THE ST. JOHN'S DIVORCE CASE
VERDICT AND SEQUEL.

The hearing of the case Duplany v. Duplany was con eluded on Monday, in the Divorce Division, before Mr. Justice Jenne and a special jury. The petition was that of Mrs. Duplany,better known as Miss Florence St. John, actress and singer, and she claimed a divorce from her husband, known in theatrical circles as M. Marius, on the ground• of cruelty and adultery. The respondent denied the cruelty, and made a counter-charge of adultery against the petitioner with Mr. Arthur Cohen, financial journalist, which the petitioner and Mr. Cahen denied. The jury retired to consider their verdict at ten minutes past four, and returned into court at twenty minutes past five o'clock on Monday evening. In reply to the court official, they stated that they found that the respondent had committed adultery, but that he was not guilty of the cruelty alleged. They also found that the petitioner and Mr. Cohen had not committed adultery This was practically a vez diet for the respondent. The adultery being proved against the respondent, Mr. Kisch, on behalf of the petitioner, asked for a judicial separation on that ground under the Matrimonial Causes Act. Mr. Gill opposed the application, and his Lordship said that this had better be made the subject of a separate applica- tion, as well as the subject of costs. His Lotdship, on the application of Mr. Studd, granted the intervener, Mr. Cohen, his costs. The result was greeted with applause, and Mr. Marius was the subject of congratulation by his friends in court. JUDICAL SEPARATION. On Tuesday morning,Mr. Inderwick, Q.C.' on behalf I of Miss Florence St. John, applied before Mr. Justice Jeune, sitting in the Divorce Court, for a decree of judi- cal separation from her husband,M. Marius. The learned council said the jury in the suit yesterday, found a ver- dict that the respondent had been guilty of adultery,but not of cruelty, and that petitioner had not been guilty of adultery. Upon these findings he asked for a judi- cial separation, giving the custody of the children to the petitioner and such costs as the taxing master might find due on these items. His Lordship inquired whether he had power to make the order when the wife had separated herself from her husband. Mr. Inderwick re- plied that there had been no real separation. There had been proposals to prepare a deed, but they were broken off on the question of the custody of the child. The di- vorce suit was shortly afterwards commenced. The adultery by the husband was not condoned adultery. Mr. Gill submitted that there had been desertion on the part of the wife for between two and three years. Mr. Inderwick said if at any time the parties wished to live together again the judicial separation would be no bar. Mr. Gill for M. Marius, asked his lordship to dismiss the application with costs. His Lordship holding that this was a case in which the court could properly exercise its jurisdiction,made the order for judicial separation,giving the mother the custody of the child, and directing that each party should pay their own costs.

M. Marius (writes a London correspondent) will have the luxury of paying Mr. Arthur Cohen's costs, but the public are chiefly concerned with the fact that it has taken seven days to try the issue. Does anyone believe that if the case had been tried in a country assize town that somehow or other it would not have been disposed ain a day or a day and a half ? The costs in this case will be considerable. Sir C. Russell, Q.C., had marked on his brief 100 guineas, with thirty guineas a day as a refresher; Inderwick, Q.C., fifty guineas, and twenty guineas a day refresher. Mr. Gill only got a twenty-five guineas brief, with ten guineas refresher. By arrange- ment the jury received one guinea per diem.

div.head: MA.SSETTLAND, MEXICO.
div.p: MA.SSETTLAND, MEXICO.
BY H. WHITHAM.

Since last writing you, several little matters have worked a change in my fortune. I wish I was able to say Dame Fortune had changed her mind, and had resolved to leave me to my own devices for the future. I cannot say that, and perhaps it is best so. Any way, at the present time lam on board the City of New York, having parted from my dear wife and children, for an indefinite length of time, and here, once more in a steerage, I am on my way to the Isthmus of Pamama with the pos- sibility of ultimately landing in New York. But it is net of this journey I propose to write now, but of the one I made

TO PIJGBT SOUND and which brought out statements I had to make in I my former letter. 1 left San Francisco on the 3rd of Nov., by the S.S. Haytian Republic, crossing a portion of the Pacific Ocean. We, after four days steaming, made Puget Sound. Steerage fare from the city to the Sound is 325. Four years ago I thought I had made up my mind as to my future steerage travelling. I thought the experience I ' had had of the Egypt was enough for a lifetime. How soon we forget these things; here I was again in a steerage differing only in one respect from my old friend: we had no lousy Jews, but were a lot of nice sociable fellows, all determined to be agreeable. I cannot say anything about the. food : I never touched it. I cannot say much about my own sociability, for the rolling of the vessel completely unfitted me for either taking food or making friends, but the rest of the good fellows seemed to enjoy themselves. Leaving San Francisco on the Tuesday, it was Friday at midnight before I felt disposed to remember that I had a stomach. What I brought from the city in this same stomach of mite 1 freely gave to the fishes. If I could have prepared them more food I would have done; un- fortunately I could not, and oh, the joys of .1.-3knogQ with an empty stomach—who can tell them At Port Angelos we stopped for two hours to discharge cargo. Amidst a drenching rain I took myself into the town to find something tempting to eat. There is not much difference made in these places between day and night; one is always sure of eithe: grocery or saloon. I found the former and was soon dis- cussing the merits of a small can of oysters. This pulled me together a little, and when we made Port Townsend abnut three o'clock in the morning I was ready to do ample justice to a good hot bowl of oyster stew. After this I pulled up fine, and my shipmates could scarcely credit that I had gone nearly five days without food. Saturday noon we

LANDED AT SEATTLE The steerage passengers had all left San Fran- cisco for the Sound to seek work in their different ways. For an hour or two I kept company with an Englishman. Poor fellow, when, I suggested a breakfast,he said he was'nt hungry; when I pressed it, he told me he had not a cent. His luggage was on the ship ; he couldn't bring it off. I was not the most unhappy man in Seattle that day. However, he got out of his difficulty before I left him. 1 met him again, a few days after; he was still seeking work, but he said he was "afraid people didn't have new clothes, so tailors were not wanted in Seattle." How I went on, and what I saw in this far away region I have already told you, and on the Bth. I think, I left Washington Territory for Portland,Oregon. I can say nothing of this journey, as it was made in the night and through a drench- ing rainy night for those who were out in it. People said it had rained for five weeks without ever a stoppage. How many miles it is from Seattle to Portland I cannot say,and I may just say here th at when I got home I had gone a round of over 2,000 miles. I had a day to spend at Portland, and what a day it was, rain, rain, rain; nothing but rain. To understand just what this means you must know that not a street in most of these cities is paved. Just enough is fixed for the cars to run on, and passengers mount at the crossings. What I saw of the city was from the cars, and I have nothing to say in its favour. Under the awnings at every saloon were to be seen scores of men standing. This is a lumber district, and rain is not a welcome visitant in a lumber camp. Thousands of penniless men are here, not knowing which way to turn,and ready at any time to make an honest penny out of a tender- foot. When I had to leave Portland things were look- ing serious with me. They say railway travelling in this country is cheap ; it may be so, but distances are something prodigous. I was at least a thousand of miles away from home. I had not more than .E 3 10s. on me, the fare was 16i dollars,and food to buy for Lhr fuur days' travelling? There is a peculiar I institution in thits-eountry travelling.Any one taking a through or round ticket from or to any given point may and often does change his mind and break his journey. What re- mains of the ticket is sold at a " scalper's " office for what it will bring. This is against railway law, of course. The ticket is then re-sold at a reduced price, the purchaser running the risk of detection at the hands of a lynx-eyed detective conductor. If found out the train is stopped and the poor beggar is pushed off wherever the train may be, losing everything he has pafd and possibly his luggage. Well, I determined to risk it, and bought one for four dollars less than the right fare. What I went through over that ticket I must not tell for my own credit's sake. I went through the ordeal suc- cessfully, and left Portland a little easier in mind. than I entered it. And now commenced the grandest and

MOST ENJOYABLE BIT OF TRAVELLING I ever made. Nor the weary desert now; but gran( majestic forest scenery, mountain scenery in all its I splendour, on every side, the rain left behind. For hours we could stand• out on the platform : it was really something to make an old man like me young again. Crossing the Siskiyow mountains is some- thing for one to remember. With two poweriul engines we commenced the winding track over the mountains. :Round and round, the train winds, every opening in the wood up above showing us the track we should by and by be steaming along, until, being at the top, we could look straight down the mountain side; and seeing no less than four lines of rail, running parallel to each other, but separated by wide distances, we knew what the switchback railway, one of the engineering wonders of the world, was. Winding down again, by the same process,we soon came in sight of Mount Shasta an isolated and extinct volcano mountain affording the finest views to be had from any mountain in North America, Its summit is covered with perpe- tual snow. From three to four hours the train winds about this mountain. I should like to dwell upon it,l don't mean tolive upiin it; but must wind up as lam writing under difficulties. The waves have just come through the port hole, and washed my desk. Leaving Mount Shasta, we head straight for Frisco, but not before the conductor tells us we may have five minutes at the Shasta Soda Springs. Just fancy us all rushing out of the cars furnished with cups and ladles, a beautiful moonlight night, and in the midst of a forest abounding with game 'of all kinds, including plenty of grizzlies. The soda water was fine; I think! should take the pledge if that water was always around. Close by runs the iSacramento river, stinlcing as the people said with trout. Well 1 have SEEN CALIFORNIA AT LAST. During the past month I have, on the Snohonish river, sat and watched the red man in his hollowed boat, as he paddled through the rushing stream. I have watched the Squaw with her papoose fastened behind her. it all seems strange. However these •red men could have lived in the old days seems beyond belief, but they are passing away, and a keener, and possibly a more savage race, is taking their place. From what! have seen I conclude that these towns, and cities, now nothing more than mere collection of wooden shanties, will in a few years be the centres of trade. You in England are helping it on, by processes to which I may not now refer. All being well, my next letter will relate what I see during this voyage, and touching at Mexican ports.

div.head: SUICIDE OF I MARRIED COUPLE.
div.p: SUICIDE OF I MARRIED COUPLE.

An elderly married couple named Lewsey, employed as caretakers at 88, Chancery-lane, London, were found dead on Tuesday, under circumstances pointing to suicide by poisoning. The only reason assigned for the double act of self-destruction is that Mr.and Mrs.Lewsey • were in such a state of health as would not permit their carrying on the duties they had hitherto discharged. The police, who are in charge of their apartments, are satis- fied that such is the cause of the tragic eiient.

div.head: PICTURE OF " SAPPHO,"
div.p: THE PICTURE OF " SAPPHO,"

A painting of extraordinary merit and beauty is now on exhibition at the Masonic Rooms, Sankey- st., Warrington. It is a study of the nude by Chevalier Ward Robertson,which has been exhibited in Paris, and in other parts of the continent, as well as in the most important towns in this country. It has elicited the highest praise from the most celebrated art critics. The "Sappho "represented is not the" counterfeit presentment S' of the poetess of classical history, but a type rather of modern beauty with modern accessories. "Sappho " is depicted, as reclining on a couch, and gazing for the moment at her own beauty, as reflected in a mirror before her. It is a matter of course to say, that the subject is one which it is difficult to treat with refinement, but it must be said that in this respect the artist has admirably succeeded. The expression is as innocent as the face is beautiful, while the figure is posed and outlined with great delicacy, and yet with striking realism. The small table at the foot of the couch, and upon which a shaded lamp and a number of roses are painted, is executed so powerfully that it is difficult for the spectator to believe that he is looking at painted and not at real objects, and so with the curtain in the back- ground, and the rug which drapes the couch. Not less cleverly and beautifully executed is the cushion upon which" Sappho" reclines. It is a marvel of brilliant colouring and realistic effect; indeed the whole painting is one which may be said to be unique as a work of art. The picture is effectually staged and brilliantly lighted. By way of adding to the interest of the visit, a courteous attendant gives an account of the picture, and organ recitals are given at intervals.

div.head: ALLEGED SLANDER OF A CROFT
div.p: ALLEGED SLANDER OF A CROFT
HORSE DEALER.

At the Nisi Prins Court, Liverpool, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Collins and a Common Jury, the case of William Sankey, a farmer, of Heath Farm, Croft, near Warrington, against Riley Elliott, a horse dealer, to re- cover damages for slander was heard. Mr. Pickford was for the plaintiff and Mr. C. A. Russell for . the defendant. Mr. Pickford said lhe pinintiff had been In the habit of sell- ing horses to the Manchester Corporation for the Scavenging Department. The defendant had also some horses. On April 21 plaintiff was at Lincoln fair, where he was consulted by the members of the committee who bought horses for the Corporation. While plaintiff was pointing out some horses the defendant came up and said he had robbed the Manchester Corporation and was a thief.—The defendant pleaded that the words were said in anger and were not defamatory, but the plain- tiff was obliged to bring the action in order to clear his character, as the Corporation told him they would not deal with him if he did not bring the action to clear him- self .—The plaintiff stated that he was at Lincoln fair on April 21st, and he :there met Alderman Robinson, Councillor Tunstall, and Mr. Whiley, superintendent of the Health Department. They were attending the fair for the purpose of buying horses. He went with them to various horses. He had before sold horses to them, but not advised them. In going through the fair he came to some horses belonging to a Mr. Gray. The de- fendant came up and said to him in the presence of the committee, "It's that long Sankey. You are at your same old game as you were last year. You robbed the Corporation out of £5 a horse last year,and you are try- ing to rob them out of £5 again." Witness asked him what he wanted, and he replied "You wanted £25 from me last year out of five horses." He (plaintiff) told him he wanted nothing from him, that last year he (defend- ant) had sent a cheque to him for £3 and he.ha,d re- turned it. Defendant then called him a thieving black- guard. For a time after thisoccurrence the Corporation had not bought horses from him, and they only recom- menced business with him when he commenced the ac- tion in May last. After hearing the case at some length, his lordship said the action seemed to be the result of a vulgar row between the horse dealers in the streets of Lincoln.—The jury found for the defendant,and his lord- ship gave judgment.

At Glamorganshire' assizes, on Thursday, Justice Vaughan sentenced James Downey, dock labourer, to seven years' penal servitude forshooting his wife and Constable Lee at Cardiff on October 16th, and Wm. Botterill, miner, to three years' penal servitude for shooting three persons at Cymmer.

div.head: COMMON CAUSE OF DEATH.
div.p: A COMMON CAUSE OF DEATH.

IS BRIGHT'S DISEASE CURABLE ? (Family Doctor, November 7, 1891.) As showing the increased attention which the public now eviuce in such matters the London "Evening News and Post" devoted a whole column of its issue of August 10th to a resume of the opinions of English and foreign specialists on the important question, " Is Bright's Disease curable ?" In view of the generally accepted opinion and belief that there is no help for a patent whose case has been diagnosed as Bright's disease, and which opinion and belief is, we make bold to say, fostered by the medical profession, it must have been with surprise that the readers of that most interesting article learned that such shining lighte as Sir Morell Mackenzie, Dr. Macla- gan, physician to the Princess Christian and other members of the Royal Family, Dr. Samuel Mills, Dr. Herbert Tibbetts, and her medical men of prominence in London, express the opinion that while some phases are incurable, others are certainly curable, or that life may be at least prolonged for a longer or shorter period. This opinion is also held by Doctors Dujardin Beaumetz, Bouchard, Labadie-Lagrave, and Professor Lepine, of Paris, Professor Senator of Berlin, and Pro- fessors Nothnagel, Schroetter, and Winternits,of Vienna. One eminent gentleman, Professor Germain Lee, of the Academie de Medicin, of Paris, calls attention to the fact that the presence of albumen in the urine does not necessarily denote Bright's disease—a mistake that is too frequently made by the ordinary practitioner. It must be a matter of self-commendation to the pro- prietors of Warner's " Safe " Cure to note that in ex- pressing the opinions referred to, the medical gentlemen mentioned but line out the arguments and mode of treatment followed by Messrs. Warner with such won- derful sucess for some years. There can be no doubt that to Messrs. Warner's persistent efforts to educate the people as to the functions and importance of those great organs the kidneys and the liver, considerable attention has be4a directed to them, and as such knowledge is of a most desirable character, we cannot but sympathise with the result of their efforts. That they are success- ful we cannot doubt, when we notice the referenee to thi_that has recently appeared in the financial jour-
While on the subject of Bright's disease, we repro- duce a testimonial of recent date, the original of which we have seen, and which we have every reason to be- lieve is genuine.

Birley Carr, Wadsley Bridge, Sheffield, October -3rd, 1891. I will relate just the bare facts of my case, and wil, say that no swearing to statement will be necessary, for some hundreds of people can bear witness as to its truth. Three years ago fever broke out in our neighbourhood and my children were attacked with it. An anxious time followed—night and day I nursed them till my strength gave way. My legs swelled with the constant wear upon them, and a large abscess forming upon one, I was obliged to take to my bed. Whilst lying there typhoid fever attacked me, and I was unconscious for four weeks. When the fever left me, I was informed by the doctor that Bright's disease had settled in my system—then dropsy set hi. From that time life was a torment, and not to be desired. My body swelled to an enormous size. I was tortured with excruciating pains. Although swollen to such a size, the doctors (I had now two in attendance) would not tap me. " I was no use," they said, " the kidneys being entirely useless, I would make water as fast as it was drawn from my body." then I begged my old doctpr to tell me the worst, so he told me there was no possible hope, I had but a few days to live, and all he could do now was to make them pass as easily as possible. Day by day he said the end was noarer, and I was glad, for two of my children had died whilst I lay there, and I did not want to live. At last but one more day's life seemed left to me. Both doctors had tried everything in their power, and both said that twenty-four hours must see the end. Still,l was to have one more chance. Taking my husband aside, my old doctor said, "There is an American named Warner, who advertises that he can cure cases of Bright's disease by means of his" Safe" Cure. He had not much faith in it ; but we could try it if we liked; it could do no harm, and it might do good. But there was no time to lose, and in the meantime he would send round some medicine. The doctor then left, and my husband rushed off to Sheffield to get the " Safe" Cure. Presently the doctor's man came with two bottles of medicine, with instructions to take some at once. I was still living when my husband returned,and gradually improved. My husband having compared the doctor's medicine with the" Safe " Cure obtained from Sheffield found them to be alike. Speaking of this to my nurse, she told me that there were three empty Warner's " Safe " Cure bottles in the doctor's :louse. :1/4) we knew for a fact that the doctor himself had as a last chance given me that" Safe" Cure. My recovery was slow, but sure. And at the end of two weeks the abscess burst. First matter and then clear water flowed, and continued to flow until my body regained its usual size, and I had no return of the dropsy. Three mouths afterwards I went down to Sheffield market. In eight months I was en- tirely recovered. Since then I have been to America and back. Such is my statement, and freely do I give you lermLision to publish it. MRS. LOUISA WOODFIELD. Witnesses I JAMES WOODvuum. 1 HENRY NATHAN'.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr. Ratcliffe presided, and there were also present, Messrs. Heaton, Hood Wright, Diggle, Mather, Clarke, Smith, Shaw, Jolley, J. W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Dobson, Kilshall, D. Jones, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), and other officers.

div.head: NEW MEMBER.
div.p: A NEW MEMBER.

The Clerk reported- t-1;t. Mr. W. J. Shaw had been duly elected in place of the late Mr. T. Jones. He men- tioned that Mr. Hickman and Mr. Smethurst had also been nominated, but he called the three gentlemen to- gether and pointed out to them the undesirability of having a contest,seeing that the election for the whole Board would take place in a few months. Mr. Hickman and Mr. Smethurst, with very good feeling,tfien took the formal course of declining to serve, in favour of Mr. Shaw.—Mr. Shaw was, on the motien of Mr. Davies, appointed a member of the House and Padgate Schocls Committees.

div.head: AN INVITATION.
div.p: AN INVITATION.

The Rev. Father it-iine";:aicie-d-the Board meeting to give an Invitation to the children of Padgate Schools, to attend a performance that evening, of the comic .opera at the Public Hall given in connection with St. Mary's Catholic Church. He thought if the Beard would allow them to attend it would be a very great treat for them. Mr. Davies moved, Mr. J. Houghton seconded, and Mr. Heaton supported, a proposal that the children be allowed to attend the entertainment. This proposal seemed to meet with general assent, when the question was raised as to the time that the entertainment took place. On its being stated that it would be 10 o'clock at night before the performance was over, the proposal was considered inpracticable and the invitation had, conse- quently, to be declined. ENTERTAINMENT FOR THB INMATES. , The House Committee recommended that an ntertain- meat be given on Christmas Day to the inmates of the male and female hospitals, subscriptions to be collected by the nurses for the purpose. The Clerk also mentioned that it was the intention of the Chairman of the Board (Mr. Balharry) to give an entertainment to the whole of the inmates.
A Bo2' DROUNED.

The CLERK said the superintendent of the Padgate School.% had received a letter from two boys who were sent to Grimsby as fisher boys stating that one cf their companions, Robert Greenway, had been Washed over- board and drowned by the • terrible gale on Thursday night last week.
DRUNKEN FEMALES.

_ The WORKHOUSE MASTER reported in his punishment book that five female inmates who had been allowed to visit Padgate schools had come home drunk. As a punishment he had put them on bread and water and set them to pick oakum for a day.—The CHAIRMAN said the House Committee had the matter before them and they had given the women a severe lecturing. ' The Committee had been considering whether it would not be better if, instead of letting the women go to Padgate to see their children, they brought the children to see them at the Workhouse.—Mr. DAVIES wished to know what Mr. Diggle thought of this case, as he seemed to think the inmates ought to be allowed out every week. It had been thought that these women should not be allowed to go out again for twelve months.—The CHAIRMAN : They have got an impression that it is not a workhouse but a palace they come to.—Mr. HEATON said that any one who misconducted themselves like that should not be allowed to go out for three menths.—lt was, however, explained to Mr. Heaton that under the ordinary rules they could not go out more than once in three months.—Mr. J. HOUGHTON : They ought not to go out for twelve months.—Mr. W. HOUGH- TON moved that the women should not be allowed out of the Workhouse for six months.—Mr. CrAnxx seconded this motion.—Mr. JOLLEY suggested that the matter should be left to the House Committee ; it would come to six months, he thought.—Mr. DrooLE thought idwould be very hard if the poor people who might not be guilty of any offence were prevented from seeing their children for six months.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON said his resolution only applied to the five women.—After some further discussion it was agreed to leave the matter in the hands of the Workhouse Master.
THN POOR-LAW CONFERENCE.

The CLERK read a report of the proceedings it the Cen- tral Peor-Law Conference held in London, which the Chairman and he had attended as a deputation from the Board. It was decided that the report should be printed and circulated amongst the Guardians.

CADBURY'S COCOA is absoluttv pure.—The Public Ana- lysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOA to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sustain- ing and nourishing beverage.--Advt.

div.head: STORM AND FLOODS.
div.p: STORM AND FLOODS.

WRECK OF A GLASGOW SHIP OFF RAMGATE. TWENTY-EIGHT LIVES LOST. On Sunday morning, while the fishing smack Bribon's Pride, of Ramagate, was making for port against a strong gale and a heavy sea, the skipper thought he .. heard a cry for help near Galloper Sands. The smack was put about, and the hands on deck saw the mast of of a ship, to which a man was clinging. It was im- possible to get near the wreckage without danger. It was not, however, until five hours later that the smacks- . men were able to launch their beat, and then William Burton, the mate, and Edwin Hurle, the third band rowed as near as possible to the standing' mast. The seaman who had lashed himself to the mizzen topmast yard sprang Into the sea, and wrs promptly rescued. He was sole ,qurvivor of the full-rigged ship Enterkin, of Glasgow,bound for Hull to Brisbane with a cargo of iron. The vessel had experi- enced very rough weather on Friday and Saturday. There was a pilot on board. On Saturday afternoon, as the Enterkin was tacking down the roadstead, she struck ehe sands. In the strong wind and with such a sea running it was seen that nothing could be done to save the ship. A short time after she struck a great sea burst upon the vessel, throwing her over upon her side. The crew sought to get into the lifeboat, which had been lowered, and which was fastened astern, but the boat was immediately swamped. Another lurch was given by the ship, and then she reeled off the sands into deep water, settling down on an even keel. The crew were thrown into the surf, and only one of those on board, an apprentice named Lewis, succeeded in reaching the mizzen spar, which was all that remained of the doomed ship above water. The number of hands, including the pilot, was thirty-one. Mr. Pollitt, the manager in Manchester of the Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway, telegraphs that the company's. steamer Asht3n, which left Grimsby for Antwerp on Saturday, saved two sailors belonging to the Enterkin wrecked on the Galloper Sands. Mr. Pollitt says the rescued men were George Gordon and Clinies Ross. both of Glasgow. WRECK OF A BRITISH STEAMER AND LOSS OF 18 LIVES. ' A Reuter's telegram received on Wednesday night from Brest states :—The English steamer Prince Soltykoff, bound from Cardiff to St. Nazaire, was wrecked on Sun- day night about six miles from Cape Usliant. Captain Flint and 17 of the crew were drowned. According to the narrative of the sole survivor, a man named Kelk, the vessel, struck by an immense wave, capsized and sank immediately. One of the ship's boats, however, remained afloat, and by means of a rope which was hanging over its side Kelk succeeded in getting into it. For thirty-two hours he drifted without food at the mercy of the waves, and was then carried by the cur- rents on to the Borsall Rocks. From these he was res- cued by some French sailors, and arrived there on Wednesday.

OTHER DISASTERS. A disastrous accident occurred on the Firth of Tay on Tuesday night. The Osprey,a large fishing boat belong- ing to Broughty Ferry, was returning home from the deep sea fishing before a strong south-east gale and blinding snowstorm, when she struck on Abertay Sands. The Osprey was manned by five hands, and it appears certain that all were lost. The floods in the Midlands are assuming grave propor- tions. Throughout the valleys ot the Ouse, the Wellaed, and the Nene thousands of acres of land are submerged. on the slopes of the valleys numbers of trees are lying about torn up by their roots or dismembered, while buildings and farmsteads are dismantled. Throughout Northamptonshire wreckage from the storms and floods lies thickly about. At Cambridge the ornamental grounds of the colleges present a sad spectacle. In Lincolnshire the deluge of rain has been varied by snow, and fields and meadows are covered with fallen trees. About a ton of lead has been displaced from the famous Boston Stump and carried away.—Mr. D. Rees, of Llanelly, who was injured by the collapse of the roof of his dwelling-house during Sunday's storm, died on Tues- day night.

div.head: RUNCORN PUBLICANS CONVICTED.
div.p: RUNCORN PUBLICANS CONVICTED.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. G. L. Davies, ,Fanny Lea, licensee of the Clarendon Hotel, Church-st., was charged with having on the sth December, unlawfully sold intoxicating liquor to two persons named George Taylor aud William Wilson. She was further charged with having permitted drunken- ness.—Mr. E. W. Humphreys appeared for the police, and Mr. A. Browne,of Warrington, defended. Mr. Browne said the first summons was not served until nine o'clock that morning, and he suggested that it should be withdrawn, and the case proceed on the question" drunk or not drunk."—Mr. Hum- phreys said the mistake. had occurred through the constable serving two copies of one summons. AS substantial justice would be done without the first summons, he would withdraw it. —ln opening the ease Mr. Humphreys said the town had got an unenviable notoriety for drunkenness, and statistics were quoted in support of that contention. It was not for the police or their advocate to secure a conviction ; it was their duty to simply lay before the Bench, the facts, and if the ' magistrates were of opinion that an offence had been committed, he asked that they should strengthen the hands of the police by inflicting such a penalty ae I would not only be a warning to the defendant, but a deterrent to others, and in the event of a conviction that the conviction should be endorsed on the license in order that the Chief Constable might have an oppor- tunity of dealing with it at the annual licensing session. —Mr. Browne: Perhaps my friend would like to hang the woman at once.—P.S. Gosling said he had been in the force 20 years, and 11 of that time as a sergeant. At 9.15 p.m. on Saturday, the sth Dec., he was passing 'the Clarendon Hotel when he heard loud talking, and a drunken man came out just as he was entering. In the bar parlour hc found both Wilson and Taylor drunk, and I with drink before them. He told Mrs. Lea that a caution had no effect upon her and that he should report the case. Mrs. Lea took no notice of the men whatever. —P.S. Woolley, an officer of 28 years' standing, 12 years as sergeant, cerroborated.—Mr. Brown, after an address for the defence, called the following witnesses :-- Margaret Johnson, of 105 Shaw-st., said she was assist- , trig defendant on the night in question. Wilson entered the house about half-past eight, and was quite sober, and she served him with a small glass of whisky. A man named Wright paid for it. Taylor came in shortly afterwards. and was also perfectly sober. She did not supply him, but she believed he was drinking from a quart supplied to another man.—William Wilson, a navvy, said he lodged in Belvedere Terrace, Cooper-st.• and that he left his loigings, between four and five o'clock, and walked about the town. He had a pint of beer with a friend, at the South Bank, and about eight o'clock he went to the Clarendon' and a man named Wright.paid for a small whisky for him. He then paid for one himself with the only twopence he had. This was all the drink he had that day. He was sober and fol- lowed the police out of the house and walked straight home. It was about 8.30 when he got home.—George Taylor, navvy, said he drank a quart of ale at his work, between eight a.m. and dinner time, and he had a pint when he arrived from the Big Field. He went to Mrs. Lea's at night, where he had glass of ale with Tom Styles, and another wltb Wright. They drank out of the same glass. This wag all the drink he had up to the police arriving. He well sober. He got back to his lodgings at half-past eight!' Charles Maidens, husband of defendant, having heel; married a fortnight said both men were sober. He coir tradicted the evidence of other witnesses in certain par ticulars.—John Stevenson, Belvedere Terrace, also swore that the men were sober.—James Brown a navvy, Joho Wright, and T. Styles gave evidence to the same effect. —The defendant also denied that the men were drunk.-' By Mr. Humphreys: She was under notice to leave the house at the present time. She received the notice before this allegation was made. She refused to state why she had to leave.—Mr. Brundrit said there had been a greet deal of contradictory evidence, but they believed the statement of the Sergeants and would fine the defendant 20s. and costs. They would not endorse the license, a*4 that was the first case against the defendant. —Wilson and Taylor were then each fined ss, and costs for being drunk.—Mr. Humphreys asked that the advocate's fee should be allowed, but the Bench declined to allow M..' Henry Hughes, landlord of the George and Dragon, Egerton-st., was charged with having on the sth Decor ber unlawfully kept a certain room in his house for pur tic music without having a license authorising him So to. do. P.S, Gosling said he visited the house on the night' in question, and in one of the rooms he found a young man playing the piano, and there were several person! there with drink before them. Defendant said he di" not know a license was required, and witness replied t that ignorance was no excuse for crime. Superintendent Large proved the publication of the advertisement an' nouncing the adoption of the Public Health (Amendment) Act.—The Bench imposed a fine of ss. and cots. and re marked that ignorance would not be accepted as a 00 in future.

The largest grain warehoue in the province are nearly empty, and people are reri duced to eating all sorts of horrible compounds as 51 stitutes for bread. A severe epidemic of small-po% raging. in two villages of Riazan. In a few weeks it 13:3, struck down two hundred persons, of whom 50 di hi Typhus is also claiming many victims in several of provinces.

WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.

• EXHIBITION OF STUDENTS' WORK. On Tuesday there was a private exhibition of students' work at the School of Art, and on Wed- nesday, Thursday, and Friday, the public were admitted free. Both at the private view and on the subsequent days there has been a large attend- ance of visitors. For s everal years back on the occasion of each annual exhibition, we have had to cbrenicle a distinct advance both in the quality and quantity of the work done at the School of Art,and this year we do not find any exception to the rule. In fact, taking the exhibition as a whole, it is indic- ative of a more than usual amount of progress dur- ing the past twelve months. The arrangement of the exhibits was similar to that on previous occa- sions. In the class room, on the ground floor, were displayed drawings by the aid of instruments, such as practical ,plane, and solid geometry—perspective, architecture, and sciography. All the work in this room was by advanced students, and some of it bad been to South Kensington and had been ac- cepted by the Department for Art class teachers' and art masters' certificates. These accepted drawings were by Stanley Pietpoint, Miss F. Jeans, H. Woodier, It. Daintith, and Miss Al. B. 'Kerry. Some building construction drawings, which had also been sent to South Kensington, and been awarded third prizes, were by L. Newcomb. Some other drawings, whose merit at once attracted notice, in- cluded a drawing of a diagonal engine to scale, by Charles F. Taylor,a section and plan of cylinder, 11. Rhodes. and also admirable drawings executed by H. Rigby and J. T. Budden. The elementary room on the ground floor contained many speci- mfins of decorative paintings, and designs for tiles, linoleums,and printed hangings. Amongst these were noticeable a fine set of six designs for tiles by J. W. Dooley, including two which have won third grade prizes and one Queen's book prize in the national competition. There were also works in decorative painting by Herbert Woodier and C. E. Jones, which had been accepted for third grade cer- tificates, and which, in the case pf that of Jones, had been awarded a third prize. Among the other ex- hibits which attracted attention were designs for cretonne and velveteen by Warren, for linoleums by Stanley Fierpoint, and decorative paintings by Arthur and Frank de Prez, a panel by Frank de Prez exhibiting boldness of outline and colouring. The studies in elemen- mentary freehand by the evenisg students, included some Rork by Ayre, of special merit, and there were some capital lrawinas by Birch, Burns, Rudd, Longdin, Daintith, and Mounfield. A set of studies of tiles of different periods by Herbert W oodier, and some histori- cal studies of decorative woodwork by Oswald Garside, had been accepted for third grade certificates. In other parts of the room there was some capital work which had been executed by M iss Ellen Cooper, J. W. Dooley, 0. Garside, H. Pierpoint , S. Pierpoint, C. E. Jones, H. Woodier, Miss Lees, and B. Daintith. Miss M. Burgess and Miss A. Chritnes contributed some studies in anatomy and other students whose work was displayed were Edith Swanwick, G. Lewis, Lily Shaw Green, Maude Gardener, Nora Fleming,Victoria Finney, May Williams, Lizzie Owen, Kate Brundrit, and Dora Hall. In tho fir3t-floor room to tlio loft of the laninii„- were exhibited models executed and cast by the students,com- prising ornamental designs, foliage, and antique figures in relief. One of these, a study of foliage from nature, by Miss Kerry, had been awarded a bronze medal, and Miss Walton, for a similar piece of work, had taken the book prize in the national competition. A model, exhi- bited by J. W. Dooley, had also taken a book prize, and in fact work of this description from the School of Art has been very successful in taking prizes offered by the Science and Art Department. In addition to the above six models have been accepted by the Department to- wards the third grade certificate, and these are by Herbert Woodier, Miss Kerry, Walter Ward, Beatrice Lees, and Frank De Prez. Other models, which seem to show an improvement on those already accepted, have already been prepared for the next eiamination by Walter Ward, Herbert Woodier, F. De Prez, and J. W. Dooley. Amongst the other exhibits in this room was a careful copy from the cast of a panel from the Church of St. Mary of Miracles, of Venice, by Oswald Garside, vase decoration by Miss Lees; some pretty plaques by Miss Walton and a needlework screen by Miss Broadbent. Miss Sylvia Breadbent, Miss Williams and Miss Ouston were also exhibitors. In the room at the other side of the landing were hung the paintings. There was a decidedly more numerous display than in previous years, and the work was probably of a dis- tinctly higher class. Mrs. Cecil Brown exhibited seve- ral very fine pictures. some of them copies of paintings in the arrington Art Gallery. Amongst these was a copy of the fine picture "Love locked out," at present in the Art Gallery. Miss Burgess and Miss A. Chrimes, as usual, were large exhibitors of creditable work, both of them being represented by figure and landscape paintings, Miss Chrimes also contributing some studies of flowers. Miss Kerry is chiefly represented by a study of dead game, a fine painting in some respects, though blemished to a certain extent by a too prominent back- ground. Miss Broadbent exhibited several sketches of scenes in Normandy, and there were also some excellent pictures from the easels of Miss Dobson, Miss Birtles, Stanley Pierpoint, Helen Cooper, Oswald Garside, Miss Walton, J. W. Dooley, Miss V. Fleming, MiS5 Schwabe, Miss Longdin, Miss Shaw Green, and Miss Lewis. On the staircase were displayed a large number of photographs brought by Mr. Aylward, the headmaster, from Paris and Venice. During the summer vacation Mr. Aylward visted the glassworks of the Company 'Venezia Murino and he was given every facility for Eve- ing the processes of manufacture carried on there. He was also furnished with many photographs illustrating " the prccesses of manufacture and the manufactured articles

div.head: CONVEItpAZIONE.
div.p: CONVEItpAZIONE.

A conversazione was held In the elementary room in the evening, at which there was a large attendance. Among those present we observed the following ladies and gentlemen :--Mr. R. Garnett, J.P.' and Mrs. Gar- nett, Mr. Councillor F. W. Monks and Mrs. Monks, Mr. Councillor Shaw Green and Mrs. Green, Mrs. Burgess, Mr. and Mrs. C. S. Burgess, Mr. and Mrs. McGregor, Mrs. Slater, Mr. R. Dobson Mr. and Mrs. H. Woods, Mr. and Mrs. H. N. Houghton, W. E. Atkin, Miss Broad- bent, Mrs. Kerry, Mrs. Cecil Brown, Miss Schwabe, Mr. and Mrs. Madeley.—Performances were given on the piano by Miss Cha.ndley-, Mrs. F. Pendlebury, Miss Tuft, and Miss Slater. There were two conjuring entertain- rnents given by Professor Frakell, and also an exposi- tion of what be called second-s!ght. His daughter had her eyes blindfolded and sat with her back to the company, while the Professor obtained from various persons in the audience articles and standinc, near the owners asked the young lady to describe' them, which she immediately and accurately , did. The Professor being a considerable distance from the platform collusion or deception was apparently impossible. Mr. Garnett handed him a railway pass and on his asking the blindfolded girl to describe what it was she did so correctly, and stated the places between which the pass was available, the class of carriage for which it was issued, the name of the company issuing it, and the name of the owner, as Indicated in writing on the pass. On this occasion the Professor was at the end of the ,room remote from the Platform. Mr. 11. Woods produced a cheque to the Professor, and she rightly declared the amount. A gen- tleman wrote several figures on a slip of paper, and the Professor handling it and requesting her to name them, she did so correctly. The performances were loudly applauded, by the perplexed and astonished audience.

div.head: OUR ALMANAC ILLUSTRATIONS.
div.p: OUR ALMANAC ILLUSTRATIONS.
ABBEYSTEAD, LORD SEFTON'S MANSION IN
WYERSDALE.

The large Sheet Almanac which we present to every purchaser of the " Examiner " to-day has for its embellishments an engraving representing the mansion of "Abbeystead," the house recently erected for the Earl of Sef ton, upon a picturesque site in the midst of his lordship's moorland estate in Wyersdale, and a vignette portrait of Lord Sef- ton. The purchase of this estate, and the building at a handsome house upon it for the noble owner's accommodation during the shooting season, are circumstances which bring into connection with a secluded district of North Lancashire a peer and great Lancashire landlord whose inherited estates lie in the south-Western corner of the county. llonours have continued to flow in upon the house of Molyneux since the baronetcy was be- stowed upon Sir Richard in 1611. His son, Richard, who had previously been knighted by James the First, succeeded to the title of baronet and to the estates on his father's death, about 1623, and not long after, on the 23rd of December, 1628, was, by Charles the First, advanced to the peerage of Ire- land with the title of Viscount Molyneux of Mary- borough. Viscount Molyneux died whilst his child- ren were young, in 1636. Richard, second Viscount Molyneux. married Frances, daughter of William Seymour, Marquis of Hertford, but had no issue. He was involved in the troubles ot the great Civil War, as was also his brotl er Caryl. They were on the King's side, and raised in 1642-3, two regiments of horse and foot, which they commanded, and served during the war. They were with Charles the Second on his passage, at the head of a considerable army, through Lancashire southward, in 1651, and were present at the battle of Worcester, in which Charles's forces were routed and dispersed. Charles William, ninth Viscount Molyneux, was created Earl of Sefton,in the peerage of I reland,3och November, 1771. Up to his time, the family had always been Roman Catholic, but this member, tha first Earl, conformed to the Church of England, in 1768, at the age of 20. His lordship died 30th Dec., 1794, leaving an only son,Williain Philip Molyneux, who succeeded him as tenth viscount and second earl,and was created a peer of the United Kingdom, with the title of Baron Sefton of Croxteth, 16th June, 1831, and died the 20th November, 1838. His eldest son was Charles William, third Earl of Sef- ton, and Lord Lieutenant of Lancashire, who died August 2nd, 1855, having married June 190,1834, Mary Augusta, daughter of Robert Cregg,Hopwood, Esq., of Hopwood Hall, by whom he had issue, sons, William Phillip; Caryl-Craven ; henry Her- vey ; Roger Gordon; and a daugh r, Cecilia Maria Charlotte ; married to the Bth Viscount Downe. The present Lord Sefton has borne numerous honours and susiained high offices, but has not been forward as a political leader, nor has he aspired to the position of a great statesman. His lordship's full title is, William Philip Molyneux, Earl of Sefton, Viscount Molyneux of Maryborough, in the peerage of Ireland, Baron Sefton of Croxteth, Co. Lancaster, in the peerage ot the United Kingdom, and a B aronet of England, K.T.S., Lord Lieutenant of Lancashire. His lordship was born on the 14th of October, 1835, and is now 56 years of age. At the age of 20 he succeeded his father, the third Earl. He was edu- cated at Eton, and entered the Grenadier Guards in 1854, became Lieutenant and Captain in 1857, but retired from the Army in 1858. Lord Seften married, 18th July, 1866,the Hon. Cecil Emily Hylton-Jolliffe, fourth daughter of tbe first Baron Hylton, and has had issue, 8029, Charles William Hylton, Viscount , Molyneux, born 25th June, 1867; Osbert Cecil born 21st February,lB7l ; and Richard Frederick, born in 1873; and daughters, Constance Eleanor, born in 1868; and Rose Mary, born in 1870. His lord- ship is patron of two Chinch livings—the vic- arages of Altcar and of Kirkby, in this county. His principal Lancashire seat is Croxteth Hall, iear Liverpool. The Croxteth estate has belonged to his family since 1459. At the date of the Parliamentary Return of the acreage and rental of landed estates in England and Wales, compiled over a dozen years since, and before his lordship's recent purchases of lands in Wyersdale, the Earl of Sefton was returned as holding 18,769 acres of land, with a total annual rental of £42,997. Lord Sefton is more of a courtier than of a keen party politician. With the members of the Royal Family he is on terms of familiar friendship. If a Liberal Government were in power which Lord Sefton could join, it would be in some ornamental office rather than any toilsome departmental post. His lordship has been a consistent member of the Whig party, but like other noblemen classed as Lib- erals, he is understood to disagree with Mr. Glad- *Zone with respect to his Irish measures. Those who enjoy the personal acquaintance of Lord Sefton think him an excellent specimen of the English nobleman,upholding in every way the dig- nity and prestige of his very ancient family ; cour- ageous and patriotic, and loyal and public-spirited, like his ancestors. Shortly after Earl Sefton acquired the Wyersdale estata he decided to have erected at some command- ing point in that picturesque valley a fine shooting box. After much consideration, his lordship decided to have the building erected on a slope above the Abbeystead Compensation Reservoir of the Lancas- ter Corporation. He placed the designs in the bands of Messrs. Douglas and Fordham, architects, of Chester, and these being approved, the contract for the whole of the work was let to Messrs. J. and W. Beanland, of Bradford, Mr. E. Wickham being the clerk of the works. The mansion—where his lordship resides in the sporting season, and at other times—was built in one of the most charming spots that could have been selected. It is near the ancient village of Abbeystead, and though only about six miles from the county town, it is quite out of the beaten tracks,the nearest railway station being five miles distant. The mansion is a commanding object for some miles round. The view from the windows of the principal apartment is delightfully varied, the valley of the Wyre stretching in front, and extended vistas of moorland, mountains, and

lake opening out to right and left. The entrance- road (on the Lancaster side) runs up into a court- yard on the northern side of the house, where the principal entrance is situated under an open porch, and separate doors round the court give access to the private, servants', and trades- men's doors. To the east is a broad, low tower, with angle turret, and a fiat roof, which is acces- sible for the enjoyment of a more extended pros- pect. The road, after crossing the courtyard, con- tinues on to the moors with an entrance to the Gun-room, &c., in the rear of the main building. On the left of this road and behind the ground rises quickly, and, from the moors above the Tarn brook, runs down and across the site to join the Wyre. The little brook is spanned by an archway, which carries the eastern wing containing Lord Sefton's Private room and Smoking-room, &c., and is itself a pleasing feature on the south front. It is (carried lorward on that side of the house, formine, an ex- tended balcony with private entrance; and with the broad terrace carried along the whole length on that front, it give a delightful promenade over- looking the dale. This terrace with its arched balus- trade,flights of steps,and piers,carrying flower vases, will aid in giving to the house that suggestion of out-door enjoyment and life which is so charac- teristic of the old English mansion. On this south- ern 'front is placed a sundial with the motto "Non numero horas visi serenas," also shields bearing the charges of the related houses, &c., the family coat- of-arms being carved over the northern entrance porch. The stone from the estate supplied the whole,of the materials of which the walls were built, <lnd out of which the mullioned windows, -copings, finials, &c., were worked. The roofs are -covered with north country green slates. The in- terior is fitted up in oak, walnut, &c., of a quiet and substantial character, and its arrangement -comprises all the conveniences required for the en- joyment and service of a country house. The stables are built to the west end of the house, and with the " Lancaster" Lodge adjoining form a Timing group of buildings.

div.head: Eetttrs to tbe attor.
div.p: Eetttrs to tbe attor.
"PROPERLY ORDAINED PRIESTS" &c.

Sir.—ln the" Runcorn and Frodsham Parish Church Magazine" for this month is the following :—" I am member of the Episcopal Church, and if I admitted a man not ordained by a bishop to minister as a priest to my family, I should be acting against my convictions. Since our Lord gave power to His Apostles, through the laying on of hands, to forgive sins, wily properly or- dained priests have inherited this gift." "You cannot get a priest ?he asked wearily." " Ah, I thought not ! Then there is no hope ; I must die without forgiveness. It is evident unto all men diligently reading the Holy Scriptures and ancient authors, that from the Apostles' time there have been these Orders of ministers in Christ's Church ; bishops, priests, and deacons." Canon Wood in his letter says :—" Here have the little ones been brought to Christ in Holy Baptism. Here have they kneeled to make their vows of service and receive the grace of Confirma- tion. Here they have together knelt before the Altar of God. Whilst we kneel devoutly at the Holy Fable. Decorations are necessary for Christmas." Such teaching as above is unscriptural. In the first place there is no such official in the Christian ministry as a priest. Will Vicars Blogg or Wood favour us with one verse out of the New Testament showing that the Apostles ever forgave sins? They cannot, yet they patronize such a worthless magazine in face of their vows " to be ready at all times to banish and drive away all false doctrine." Verily it is plain to all that in Apostolic times there was no such official as a diocesan bishop. We read of a plurality of elders at Ephesus, Crete, and Philipp (see Acts 20c. Titus lc. Philippians lc.). Bishop Mant says the word Bishop, Elder, Presbyter, are used promiscuously for one person. Canon Wood has pre- viously owned that there is nothing in the New Testa- ment for sprinking infants ; he cannot find one solitary case of an infant being sprinkled, nor can he find the rite of confirmation or the sensuous decoration of the church, and for my own part, I know not how anything should be worthy of God's accepting, that is not of God's commanding. Canon Wood calls the Lord's table an altar.; Christ called it a table. Who is right ? The word altar does not occur once in the Communion office, but he will find table mentioned a dozen times or more. God is a spirit and must be worshipped in spirit and in truth (truly) not with a few evergreens, white crosses, fruits, or flowers. We are, alas ! travelling backwards not for- wards. The" holiness of beauty" is the modern sub- stitute for the " beauty of Holiness "—the sacraments for Christ ; Church instead of the Gospel. Frodsham, Dec. 15, 1891.
ROBERT FOULKES.
SODIE GNOSTIC FALLACIES.

" Is it not a truism that without divergence from that which exists, whether it be in politics, religion, manners, or anything else, there can be no progress? "—Herbert 3pencer, "Studies in Sbmology " (P. 238.)

Sir,—My sentiments on finding such a one as" Gnos- tic," dabbling in this controversy are much like those of Pope on seeing the fly in amber :—" The thing itself is neither rich nor rare, the only wonder being—how it got there! " Anonymous writing of the " Gnostic" type raises in my mind the question :—ls the advocate ashamed of his subject, or afraid lest his subject be ashamed of his advocacy ? I see nothing shameful in

FOREIGN MISSIONARY ANNIVERSARY.

trying to get at the truth by discussion. If we state our opinions and render our reasons; if we publish both, we therefore invite all the world and his wife to show the unsoundness of such opinions and the invalidity of the reasoning. By so doing we apply the touchstone of adverse criticism, and bring our reasoning into contact with widely divergent intellects by which new light may be thrown upon them or the reasoning itself overthrown and refuted. But there are some minds so constituted as to be incapable of facing an argument. If you talk of the land tax, nothing but the discussion of window money will satisfy them. Any argument, however in- surmountable, may be surrounded by your opponents talking of something else ; albeit such evasion evinces a sad wantof self-respect and disrespect for subject and opponent. And this is emphatically " Gnostic's " method. He resembles the Irishman who captures three prisoners by surrounding them ! However right and proper as a military method ,it is, controversially, beneath contempt. My agnostic ignorance of " Gnostic's" social status leaves me at liberty to conjecture. His letters would lead me to infer that he might be in a situation enabling him to hear scientific conversation—that he has thus been at a feast of reason and . tolen the scraps ; hence his too frequent use of scientific terms—parrot-llke without adequately apprehending them. Judging frctn his vaguely didactic style, I infer that he relieves the mono- tony of his calling by excursions as a " local " into the regions of inconsequent homiletics. From his frequent misuse of the term knowledge it is evident that our" pure scientist " does not sufficiently distinguish between what we know and what we im- agine. We are told "it would sweep from the domain of knowledge such subjects as God, the soul of man, &c." Now as these subjects never were in the domain of science, they cannot be swept from it. Not only do we not know God, but the idea of the Infinite is altogether inconceivable by our finite faculties. Again, what do we" know "of the soul, as dissociated from mind, of which it is but a manifestation ? Further on we are , informed that the soul is "self-poised, and acts from within. This is also the definition of " perpetual motion," and hence it is singularly appropriate as des- criptive of another non-entity.: But such trifling lapses from "," pure science ": may surely be excused in the man who can conceive matter as immortal ! " Science, moreover," says "Gnostic," proposes to regard the atom as indestructible, and therefore immortal," (sic, my italics). Our old friend "any schoolboy" would have got a well-deserved birching for such a sentence. Imagine science abrogat- ing its right to the title by entertaining such evidently absurd ideas as the immortality of dead matter ? Hence we have the reduetio ad absurdant :—dead matter is immortal—therefore " why should it be regarded as absurd to maintain the immortality of the soul ?" Now science does declare matter indestructible, but leaves its eternity and immortality to occupy the bemused faculties of the gnostic. In taking final leave of this pale shade of reason— this wandering spirit whose attenuated form has been so long familiar to us, I would remind him that I am still ignorant of any logic countenancing prayer for fair weather. And it was this state of ignorance that he, by implication, led us to infer that he could en- lighten. Whore then is "the logic deductive or induc- tive "which he would have us believe was at his finger ends ? Is he still "touring round " in search of it ? As I cannot wait, believe me, yours &c.. JOHN PEERS. Penketh, 6, 12, 1891.

div.head: BAND OF HOPE MEETING.
div.p: BAND OF HOPE MEETING.

On Friday evening, a public meeting of the Wes- leyan Band of Hope was held in the Wesleyan Day School. The meeting was presided over by Mr.C.E. Parker. An excellent programme, consisting of solos, glees, recitations, dialogues, &c., was gone through by the members of the Band of Hope, as- sisted by some of the elder friends, and much ap- preciated. Mr. R.H. Posnett delivered an excellent address on the benefits of total abstinence. Votes of thanks to the chairman and choir concluded the meeting.

div.head: TECHNICAL CLASSES.
div.p: TECHNICAL CLASSES.

On Monday e;;;;;-ing—ti public lecture, on "The science and art of dressmaking," was delivered by Mrs. Dobson, in the infant school. Admission was free. There was a good attendance,numbering about 50. Miss Tinsley presided, and introduced Mrs.Dob- son. Mr. J. Forster and Mr. Dignum, two members of the committee, were present. Mr. Foster said he hoped the class would be appreciated and well a. - tended. At the conclusion of the lecture, about 20 joined the class. As there are many dressmakers in Penketh, the class should prove very popular.

div.head: MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.
div.p: MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.

The usual weekly meeuing of the above associa- 7jQy G V fX in f hes Woo- leyan Schoolroom. There was a moderate atten- dance. The evening was described in the syllabus as a "miscellaneous "one, Mr. 11. J. Jones, who was responsible for it,taking the chair. On Wednesday Mr. Jones introduced a novel feature, as, instead of having one of the usual musical evenings,he induced several young ladies to write short papers. These he read himself, suppressing the names of the au- thors. As each paper was read, an interesting dis- cussion followed.

div.head: POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS.
div.p: POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS.

For some time past there has been a growing feeling at Penketh that a letter box was required at the Widnes end of the village. Some time ago, the post office, which was practically in the centre of the village, was removed to one of Mr. Rogers's houses, considerably nearer Warrington. This re- moval caused some inconvenience to a number of the villagers at the west end of Penketh,who,wish- ing to post a letter, had to go to the post office to do so. To remedy this, Mr. Kerry, postmaster of Warrington, has, it is stated, decided to place a pillar lecter box on the Warrington road, near the Crown and Cushion. This is to be done immediately, and the box will shortly be fixed ready for use. It is to be emptied each evening at 7 40 p.m. ; letters to be posted later must be taken to the post office. The box there closes at 840 p.m. For the conveni- ence of those residing near Fiddler's Ferry station.a letter box was placed there about two years ago. It is emptied each evening at 7 40 p.m.

div.head: FOREIGN MISSIONARY MEETING.
div.p: FOREIGN MISSIONARY MEETING.

The annual foreign missionary meeting in connec- tion with the Wesleyan Chapel, was held last Thurs- day evening, the chair being taken by Mr. Robert Shaw. There was a moderate attendance. Mr. Shaw was supported on the platform by the Revs. J. Gunnell, A. Freeman, and T. Ross, and Mr. R. Garnett, and Mr. R. Cook. The annual report of the society was read by the Rev. A. Freeman, which showed that Penketh had contributed a total sum of £26 13s. 2d., being an increase over the previous year of £2 19s. 10d. This total included amongst other items the sum of .£l. 10s. 9d. as the result of the juvenile Christmas offerings in 1890, also the sum of £5, which was collected for the purpose of assist- ing to keep a native boy at one of the mission schools in India. Addresses were delivered by the Chairman, the Revs. J. Gunnell, A. Freeman, and T. Ross. Mr. Ross in speaking to the children, showed them some scrolls printed in Chinese characters and a quantity of Chinese money called "cash," which he had recently received from China. At the close of the service a collection in behalf of Wesleyan Foreign Missions was taken and realised a satisfactory amount. After a hearty vote of thanks had been accorded Mr. Shaw for his services in the chair, the meeting concluded by singing the Doxology.

div.head: MURDER AND SUICIDE.
div.p: MURDER AND SUICIDE.
A DENIENTED MOTHER'S CRIME.

On Thursday evening Mary Ann Ilamnet, wire of a faim labourer, aged 35, and her infant child, 12 months old, were run over by a Liverpool express, and nearly cut to pieces on the Cheshire Lines, at Baguley, near Altrincham. Inquiries made upon the spot yesterday morning con- firm the view of a determined murder and suicide, though the motive discovered is. very slight. The woman left home about six in the evening, taking with her the child in its nightdress, and following her husband to a grocery store, where he had gone to pay a bill. The wife was considerably in arrears with her payments. The supposition is she was afraid to meet his displeasure on discovery of her deceit. .119 w she got upon the line is a mystery. From the position in which the bodies were found immediatvly under the bridge on the western side of the railway station, the conjecture is that she first laid the child across the metals of the up line and then herself sat close to, waiting the arrival of the up train. One half of the child's body was found in the six-foot way, and the other half in the four-foot way. The body of the mother was carried ten yards nearer to the station, and was found mutilated on the up four- foot way. B

APPROACHING MARRIAGE OF THE DUKE OF CLARENCE.

The "Daily Telegraph " says :—We understand that the marriage of the Duke of Clarence and Avondale and Princess Victoria Mary of Teck will be celebrated on February 27th, in St. George's Chapel, Windsor Castle. If any change is hereafter made in this date before the final settlement of all the necessary arrangeuaents, it will probably be in favour of February 29th-1892 being of coureo leap year. No doubt the choice of St. George's Chapel, Windsor, in preference to St. James's Palace, may cause a certain amount of disappointment to the people of London, but it has the twofold merit of meeting the convenience of her Majesty the Queen and being strictly in harmony with historic prece- dent. There is, it is stated, no precedent for the marriage of a prince in liberal succession to the Crown taking place at Westminister, whereas for the celebration at Windsor there is a very recent instance to be found in the wedding of the Prince of Wales himself, which was celebrated there on March 10, 1863. Fortunately, however, the arrange- ments in prospect will enable the inhabitants of the capital to take their part on the auspicious occasion. Although no place has been selected for the honeymoon, it is understood that the Royal pair will not go to the Continent, but will remain in this country, and possibly at Sandringham. In this event they will, after the wedding, return to Paddington, and from there proceed in open car- riages with an escort to St. Pancras or some other Metropolitan terminus, and so pass through several of the principal thoroughfares of the capital. In view of these arrangements, the wedding ceremony will, we believe, be performed at a somewhat earlier hour than is customary at Royal martiages, pro- bably before noon, in order that the procession through the streets of London may take place in good daylight. The young Prince has been in love with Princess May for three or four years, and according to the tittle-tattle of the hour, the truth is he some months since intimated that, unless the Princess became his wife, he intended to remain unmarried. The intimation did not cause any particular sensation among the members of the Royal Family ; but when Prince George af %tales fell ill, and it was realised what might happen if only the life of Prince Albert Victor intervened between the succession and the Fifes, the Queen and the Prince and Prin- cess of Wales altered their minds. Objection has been taken on the score of relationship, and on the ground that the young lady is not English. But it is far better for second cousins once removed than for own cousins to marry. The Princess May has as much English blood in her veins as the Prince, and she has certainly spent most of her time among the English people. As the 27th falls on a Satur- day, the usual half-holiday would afford to many thousands, more than on any other day, the oppor- tunity to witness the procession. The Princess May, as she is always called, an im- provement on her formal address, is perhaps the most popular of the younger generation of Royal prett3, piquante, well dressed (a circumstance which,as tto auhguters ot Christian testify, is not a matter-of-course with Royal Princesses), has all the happy nature of her mother and something of the abounding bonhomie of her father. This is the positive aspect of the ad- vantage of the match. As has been shown in the case.of the Princess of Wales it is of enormous sup- port to the Lteir Apparent to have for a wife a lady who appeals directly to the affection of the public. For this Princess May, whether ranking as Duchess of Avondale, Princess of Wales, or the Queen of England, may be counted upon. The young Princess shares one immeasurable ad- vantage possessed by the Queen up to the eve of her ascending the Throne. For some years her Majesty did not stand in direct succession, her father being the fourth son of George 111., with George IV. on the Throne, and the possibility of issue to the Duke of York and the Duke of Clarence barring the way of the little daughter of the Duke of Kent. To the Princess May this opening of the prospect to the steps of the Throne has been even more sadden and unexpected than was that which dawned on the Princess Victoria of Kent. Hitherto she has stood on the extreme outer edge of the Royal circle, at best a poor relation. The paternal revenues aro even more shadowy than those pertaining to the average German Princeling of the Battenberg order. Forty years ago her mother, Princess Mary of Cam- bridge, began to receive from the Consolidated Fund a pension of £3,000 a year. On her marriage this was increased to £5,000, the sum at which it

ACCIDENT AT THE WIGAN AND WHISTON COLLIERY.— As Edward Taylor, aged 40, a day wageman, employed at the Wigan and Whiston Colliery, was working on Tuesday, removing props down below, a large stone fell from the roof almost taking the flesh from his thigh and arms and laying open his nose and head. It took six men to remove the stone from him. As soon as they had got away another stone fell which, had they been under would have proved fatal to them all. The poor man is progressing favourably.
