thi- tllle to the peculiar position he holds, with his grandmother on the Thorne and his father called upon to perform the orainary functions of Royalty in its relations to the public. Nothing could be calculated as more to his advantage than the possession of such a consort as he will find in the charming, sprightly Princess May. Little more than two years ago, in the session of 1889, a Select Committee was appointed to consider and if possible finally settle the whole question of grants to members of the Royal Family. The Government have to thank Mr. Gladstone and his proposals for averting at the present junc- ture the awkward necessity of coming to Parlia- ment for a special grant on account of the Duke of Clarence and his bride. There was at first some difficulty about the precise sum to be handed over to the Prince ; .E 40,000 a year was named, and £36,000 was finally fixed upon, it being stipulated that it should be paid during the life-time of the Queen and for six months later. It is out of this money that the portion of the young couple will be provided, as was that of the Duchess of Fife. Since the Queen undertook the provision for the children of her daughters and younger sons this difficult and delicate question was finally settled for the duration of the present reign, whilst it may reasonably be expected that so wise a percedent will rule through all succeeding time. The Duke and Duchess of Clarence and Avondale will eventually take up their residence at St. James's Palace, in tln. apartments formerly occupied by the late Duchess of Cambridge. The provision to be made for the Duke of Clar- ence and Avondale has not yet been settled, but, whatever the amount may be, it will be provided out of the sum granted by Parliament to the Prince of Wales, and there will, it is stated, be no further application to the House of Commons. Princess May of Teck will be presented with her wedding dress—which is to be made of silk fabrics from British looms—by the Ladies' Committee of motion/LE Silk Association. Tuesday—nig:ht's " Londoli Gazette" announces that the Queen, in Council at Windsor, on the 12th inst., was pleased to declare her consent to a con- tract of matrimony between the Duke of Clarence and Princess Victoria Mary of Teck, which consent her Majesty has also caused to be signified under the Great Seal and entered in the books of the Privy Council. The London County Council, on Tuesday, with five dissentients, agreed to an address of congratu- lation to the Prince and Princess of Wales on the approaching marriage. A London correspondent says :—I understand that Parliament will be asked to vote a small allowance for the future Duchess of Clarence. This motion is not likely to be seriously opposed, for the Duke and Duchess will have only twenty thou- sand a year, whereas each of the younger sons of the Queen began married life with a Parliamentary allowance of twenty-five thousand, and all of them had other resources. It will also be necessary to make a provision for the future Duchess of Clarence in the event of her husband's death, as he has no- thing whatever in his power, and his income from the fund which was granted by P arliament in 1889 for the family of the Prince and Princess of Wales is only for his life.

FREE CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—A paper entitled " Will our bodies rise again?" was given in the schoolroom, last night week, by Mr. George Jones. The essayist was of the opinion that the sacred writings did not show that the natural body would rise again. A discussion then ensued, in which the Presjdent, Rev. R. Trotter, Messrs. W. Noden, H. Lewis, E. Aston, T. Jones, and J. Hancock took part. PLEASANT EVENINGS.—The attendance at the weekly concert, held on Saturday, was a great success. The programme was filled up entirely by members of the young men's Bible class, and the items comprised glees, trios, duets, songs, and readings, by Messrs. Pugh, Jones, T. rover, W. Owen, W. Foyer, G. Chatwood, J. Johnson and W. Bowden. The proceedings which were of an enjoyable character, were ably conducted by Mrs. Fair- bank, one of the teachers of the class._ . .

TRINITY MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—At the weekly meeting, Mr. J. F. Wright read his essay on " Total Abstinence, its effects," in which he stated that intoxicating drink was the parent of crime, it was the cause of bad trade in some respects; filled our prisons ; besides being injurious to health. Mr. Wright also quoted the testimonies of certain eminent medical men with respect thereto. The question was subsequently discussed by the Rev. P. Pizey, Messrs. Rhodes, Robin- son, Pickering, and W. Andrews. FREE CONCERT AT FIVE CROSSES.—Under the pre- sidency of Mrs. Firbank,an enjoyable evening was spent in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Five Crosses, on Monday. The entertainment was given in continuance of a series of monthly gatherings of the workingmen and their wives,which were organised by Mr. Isaac and a staff of willing helpers. The programme contained readings. recitations, songs, and solos, besides the " Influenza," "Laughing," and the" Japanese Fan," action songs,the whole of which were quite a success. PRIMROSE LEAGUE MEETING.—A meeting of the Frod- sham District Habitation of the Primrose League was held at the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Monday evening. Mr. J. Reynolds, J.P. ruling councillor, presided, and there was a good attendance. The minutes of the last meeting having been read by Colonel Ashton, on behalf of Mrs. Ashton, honorary secretary, and confirmed, the Chairman briefly, but feelingly, alluded to the loss they had all sustained in the death of Mr. Clarke Aspinall. After reverting to the tenets and principles of the Prim- rose League, a miscellaneous entertainment of vocal and instrumental music was gone through. During an interval in the programme, a speech was delivered by Mr rtoft. of Liverpool. on the leading political topics or tne nay, emoraLang L 6 eigi-IG hours- queSLluii, the disestablishment craze, the home and foreign policy of the Government, and their consequent influence on the trade, taxation, and prosperity of this country, the Irish question, and the liquor traffic. A cordial vote of thanks was unanimoasly passed to Mr. Croft, at the close of his speech, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Colonel Ashton, who, in a few well chosen remarks, said that in the event of the eight hours ques- tion ever becoming law, lie hoped solicitors would be left out of its operations, as it was frequently his mis- fortune to have to work considerably more than eight hours a day.

Tas POLICE COURT.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Monday, before Dr. Brabazon, Joseph Hattcn, a tramp, was charged with begging at.Heatley, on Saturday after- noon. The case was proved by P.C. Howie, and prisoner was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. CONGREGATIONAL BAND OP HOPE —An entertainment in connection with the above Band of Hope was given in the schoolroom on Monday evening, the Rev. Charles Clay, 8.A., in the chair. Mr. F. Milne, of Sale, deliv- ered an address, after which a miscellaneous programme of songs, recitations, Sce., was gone through. .

, WESIEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT gOCIETY.-A meet- ing of this society was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening, Mr. Simpson being in tha chair. Au address on " Botany," was given by Mr. Briggs, the address being illustrated with roots and plants. Messrs. Brown, E. Moston Brereton, and Thorp took part in the discus- sion that followed.

NON-MAINTENANCE.:-- Henry Percival, formerly of Lynn. now of Stockport, was summoned for non- compliance with an order to pay an amount due for maintenance of his wife, was ordered to pay in a month or go to prison for six weeks. DOGS AT LARGE.--Richard Miller, and Henry Taylor, for having dogs at large, without muzzle or collar, at Statham, and at Warburton on the 16th respectively, were fined 2s. 6d. each. _ _ _ _

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Frederick Gould, at Lymm, ss. including costs, and Charles Bowen, at Warburton, dismissed on payment of coats. CHARGE AGAINST A PIIDLICAN.—George John Harrop, landlord of the Railway Hotel, Heatley, was summoned for permitting drunkenness at his house on the Ist inst. The defendant was absent through illness.— P.C. Howie deposed to finding a man named Rowlands drunk, with beer before him, in the house about three o'clock.—Miss Harrop said there was not the slightest indication of drunkenness in the man.—Alice Winstan- ley, of the Farmers' Arms and Margaret Bell deposed t 3 seeing him drunk about ten minutes past three.—John Muldon, employed at the Railway Hotel, denied that Rowlands was drunk.—Tiae defendant was fined ss. and costs, the license not to I:4endorsed. WOMEN'S QUARRELS.—Sarah Saunders was charged with assaulting Elizabeth Fairburn, wife of a Ship Canal labourer, at Ileatley on the sth inst. Evidence was given, from ivhich it appeared that one woman was about as bad as the other, and they were each bound over in the sum of £lO to keep the peace for six months

LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDIT.—Beef: is quiet, without change in values. Pork has a slow sale at the quotations. The market for Bacon shows little or no appreciable change ou yesterday's prices. Demand is moderate in extent, and is fully met by holders. Hams Long cuts Is. per cwt. lower. shorts cuts unchanged. Shoulders steady. Cheese firm bus- quiet. Butter unchanged. Lard fractionally lower. Irnpor' of fresh beef from New York, 2,080 cwts., ditto from Philadelphia 2,450 cwts. Imports of salted provisions Beef 150 150 tierces ; pork, 307 barrels ; bacon, 1.386 boxes ; hams, 370 boxes ; cheese, 2,545 boxes ; butter, 2 packages ; and lard. 19 tons.—Cable advices from America received to-day quote lard and bacon without material change ; hogs 5 points higher. MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY.—There is no material change to report since the opening, and among producer, there is a good deal of grumbling and selling. In cotton more activity has been developed, since the opening, and the esamate of spot transactions has been raised from 10,000• 12,000 bales. Yarns are not greatly altered, and good twit,' . keep very steady- Common sorts tend rather in buyer's' favour, and the same may be said ot most counts of weft. Cloth is not good, but Eastern business continues to be done by easy sellers, and compared with yarns the position is much worse than say last July,

door youngsters all have it oil. One of the oldest couplets runs as follows : At Christmas, play and make good cheer, For Christmas comes but once a year. There are many versions of this well-known rhyme. The one thus rendered is attributed to Thomas Tusser who was born in 1523—forty-one years before Shakespeare—and is found in his poem of The Farmer's Daily Diet." Yet another bit of folk-lore, wilich has the merit of being local : Prescot, 11 uyton, and merry Childow, Three parish churches all in a row : Prescot for mugs; Huyton for ploydee ; Childow for ringing and singing 'besides. " Childow " is a provincialism for Childwall ; and " ploydes " is understood to be an old word for merry meetings, although some people contsnd that " ploughs" are meant. What says "the old- est inhabitant " of Huyton ? Is it beyond even his recollection?

SUSPECTED MURDER IN IRELAND. Robert Merrigan, a gamekeeper, was on Thursday night found dead at Tinahoe, Queen's County, with gun shot wounds in the head, having apparently been mur- dered. THE WATERFORD ELECTION. The Waterford nomination is fixed for next Tuesday, and the polling for the following day. The poll will be declared late the same night. Mr. Austin, Labour Com- missioner, is workigg on behalf of Mr. Davitt. ROYAL MOVEMENTS. The Queen and Princess Henry of Battenbeg and her children, with the suite, left Windsor, yesterday for Gos- port, via Basingstoke. The Queen and party reached Gosport at 12 30, and left for Osborne, aboard the royal yacht. The war vessels in the harbour were, decorated, but fired no salutes. PRINCESS MAY'S WEDDING DRESS. Lancashire, and not Spitalfields, is having the honour lof manufacturing Princess May's wedding dress. The material ha already passed through the loom at Messrs. Robinson and Millington's silk mill, Patricroft, near Manchester. The pattern is a very elaborate oHe with a wreath of roses and rosebuds in the centre, the material being white silk broche. Naturally the weavers are much pleased that the establishment has been thus honoured. NEW TREATIES OF COMMERCE. BERLIN, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—The Reichstag to-day .after a somewhat lively debate approved the new com- mercial treaties by 243 to 48. The fagiires were received with loud cheers.

BOROUGH OF '", • v WARRINGTON. , , BANK HOLIDAY, 26TH, DECEMBER 1891. I have been requested by a deputation representing the Tradespeople of the town to GIVE PUBLIC NOTICE, that It is their desire and intention to observe SATURDAY NEXT, the 26th instant, as a BANK HOLIDAY. I. therefore, request all Manufacturers and Shopkeepers to Close their Places of Business on that day, and afford their Assistants and others the opportunity of availing themselves of the Holiday. EDWARD GREENALL, Jun., Mayor. Town Hall. Warrington. 19th December, 1891.
